Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 100) to amend the Pilotage Act.
Will the hon. minister explain ?

The Bill is a very simple one ; it is only to authorize the Governor General in Council to constitute the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the officials of his department the pilotage authority for part of a harbour under the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners. A difficulty has presented itself in regard to the application of the law which was passed last session regarding the Saguenay river. The pilotage authority for that river was formerly vested in the harbour commissioners of Quebec. With the consent of all the parties interested, the law was amended and the pilotage authority of the Saguenay river, part of the district formerly under the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners of Quebec, was put under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Unfortunately in that Bill it was not provided that the pilotage authority should be vested in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, so when the law came to be applied as regards the regulation and examination of pilots, it was found that the Minister of Marine could not act. It is to obviate this difficulty, which may also present itself in other cases, that the Bill is introduced.
It puts them all under the authority of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

No, as it may be in the interest of navigation the Governor General in Council may constitute the Minister of Marine the pilotage authority for a part or the whole of a harbour which is under the control of commissioners.
Any harbour in Canada ?
Any harbour in Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

(Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 101) to amend the Steamboat Inspection Act, 1888. He said : The effect of the Bill is :
To provide for the inspection of the machinery and equipment of steamboats propelled by gas, fluid, naphtha, electricity, or any other mechanical or chemical power, and in the case of such vessels for making such changes in forms A and B of the second schedule hereto as he deems advisable.
Hitherto these boats could not be legally examined under the law as it exists, and, as with modern progress, many of these boats are now on the water, it is thought to be in the public interest that they should be subject to inspection when required.
Those boats that are not let out for hire, such as private yachts and boats, are they subject to inspection too ?
Not those that are used for pleasure, hut those that may be hired or may be used for the ferrying of people from one place to another, or for excursions will be subject to inspection.
Private yachts will not be subject to inspection ?
If they are used for these purposes they will be.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does this apply to gasoline launches as well ? If it does, I want to inform the minister that among the Thousand Islands on both sides of the river there are thousands of these little yachts propelled by gasoline engines and I know that a commotion will be raised if the hon. gentleman tries to interfere with the gasoline yacht. Many of these private yachts on both sides of the river do more or less ferrying.

If they are used for conveying the public surely the public is entitled to be protected. If these boats are let out, or a charge is made for ferrying people, I think they should be put on the same footing as other boats used for the same purpose.

Does the hon. gentleman propose to grant certificates ? I know of cases where boats were used for hire and for carrying passengers, where the inspectors for the Marine Department refused to make an examination or to grant certificates. Is this to meet difficulties of that kind and to grant certificates in future where the men are up to the standard ?
Exactly. It is to meet these demands that are made at different times for the inspection of machinery and equipment of these boats.
Is any provision made for the examination of the officers and engineers in charge ?
Yes, of course, there is provision to grant certificates to the mechanics who are employed on board those boats.

I would like to ask the hon. minister whether or not the Bill is founded on any investigation and report of the officers of the hon. gentleman's department ? Might I also suggest that if the Bill is founded on any such report it would be wise to have the report laid on the table of the House for the information of those who may desire to discuss the measure.

Certainly. When the Bill comes before the Committee of the Whole House, all the information will be given. This Bill is not introduced of my own motion or because of my experience ; it is introduced because it has been recommended by the officers in charge of this part of the department. But complaints of this kind Mr. CLARKE.
have been reported to me, and I have also been many times approached directly to have such a law as this passed to remedy the existing defect.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if his amendment covers the case of a steam launch towing a string of fishing boats or pleasure barges or in work of that kind ?
It would cover them all if they were for the use of the public and for hire.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are many hired in this way : I go to a livery and hire a boat for the day. That is my boat for the time being and not subject to inspection. It is my property for that day. There are hundreds of them used in that way by livery men all along the river. You go to a boat house and hire a row boat or gasoline launch for a day. Is it the intention to make the law applicable to these launches which are simply hired out in the same way as a horse and buggy ?

The point will have to be considered when the Bill comes before the Committee of the Whole, but I am quite sure it would be advisable that such boats should be inspected. I do not think the hon. gentleman would like to use the boat that had not been inspected and thus expose his precious life upon the waters.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have to have an army of officers to inspect them all. It will put the people who have been using these boats for several years to-a great deal of inconvenience.

I would like to ask the hon. minister, if, in the framing of this Bill, the representations which have been made to the department during the past three or four years by the society of Marine Engineers have been taken into consideration ?

The Bill is the result of representations by different parties-people owning boats, people using them and people who are asking for certificates, or asking that their boats should be inspected. We cannot at present provide the necessary inspection certificates nor the necessary certificates for the men operating these boats. When the Bill is considered all the circumstances and all the facts will be put before the House. I came to the conclusion that a law of this kind would be in the public interest.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for

leave to introduce Bill (No. 102) to amend the Shipping Casualties Act 1901.
Will the hon. minister please explain ?

This Bill is rather important in that it provides that in case an accident happens to a steamboat the officer charged with the investigation, as regards the master and mate, will be empowered to investigate at the same time the case as regards the pilot. At the present time, if an accident happens and an investigation takes place at once by the order of the minister, the official who makes this investigation is entitled to proceed with the investigation as regards the master and mate, but if he discovers the fault is due to the pilot, he has to hold another investigation afterwards. Under this Bill the officer charged with the investigation, upon discovering, during the course of the investigation that the pilot is at fault, will have the right to notify the pilot according to law and put him on his defence. It will avoid the trouble of having two investigations for the same accident. When the Bill comes before the Committee of the Whole, I will be in a position to give a further explanation and go into the matter more in detail.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
