House in Committee of Supply.
Northwest Mounted Police-pay of forces, $205,000.
["Very well, we will call it six o'clock.\nAt six o'clock committee took recess. After Recess.\nHouse resumed at eight o'clock."]

We ask for an increased vote of $100,000 this year to provide for 100 extra men. The old members of the ETouse will rememuer, that when the force was first organized in 1873, it was composed of 1,000 men. In 1892 or 1893 the force was decreased to 700. and in 1895 it was further decreased to 500 which is the number to-day. The rapid growth of the country, however, requires an increase of [DOT]100 men, and we have concluded to ask parliament for this extra appropriation. The force to-day has posts ranging from near Emerson in Manitoba, through the Northwest Territories, and north to the mouth of the MacKenzie river. There are eighty posts in all, and at some, there are sixty or eighty men, while at others there are only two men, and at some only one man. I have here two^ maps which show the territory over which the force is distributed, and hon. gentlemen can inspect them if they take an interest in it.
Does the 500 include those in the Yukon ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. The duties of the police are of a very complex character. They have to protect property, and they have to guard the Indians, who at present give very little trouble, I am glad to say. The police have besides, to protect settlers, to guard against fires, to aid in the protection of the public health, and although there is, I am happy to say,

not much to do in the way of keeping ol der among the new settlers, yet the police are very useful in teaching them how to assimilate themselves to the requirements of the country.
The police duties are no greater than they always have been, and the territory is not any larger.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The territory is not larger, but the population is much larger.
I hope you are not getting in immigrants who require the police to keep them in order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad to say that the new population does not necessitate any increase in the force in the way of maintaining law, but if you tell the people of the Northwest that you are in favour of decreasing the force,' I do not think you would be very welcome amongst them. We have tried again and again to reduce the force, but we have come to the conclusion that on the contrary, it is necessary to increase it.
Have the mounted police in the Yukon any special duties which are not discharged by the police in the Territories ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

This appropriation for the Northwest Mounted Police has now reached the large sum of half a million dollars. I have a distinct recollection that some years ago. very .pointed criticism was launched at the government of the day for maintaining so large a force, it being claimed that with proper management of the country, there was no need for so many policemen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not re-, member that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) ever made that criticism.

No. But the member for South Oxford (Sir Richard Cartwright) usually indulged in it, and it was said that as settlement increased and civilization advanced, there could not be any trouble caused by the wild men of the plains, and that we should reduce the force. It would r.ow appear that as the settlement increases the number of policemen requires to be increased. It may be necessary, but I would point out to the Prime Minister that if he gave provincial autonomy to the Territories, he would be able to reduce this vote very materially.

I notice that the appropriation is increased by one-fourth although the force Is not increased by one-fourth. There seems to be a disparity in the proportions there. Would the right hon. gentleman say if any new equipment is required this year besides that for the additional

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: men who are coming in ? The expenditure is increased by $67,500. It would seem that the increase of $22,500 is for the pay of the additional force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At present we have 500 men, and the appropriation last year was $400,000, which would be $800 per man. This year we shall have GOO men, and the expenditure will be $833 per man. I do not think we can do better than that.
For 600 men we are requiring an additional $100,000, which is not the same proportion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, it is. The vote this year amounts to $833 per man. If you look at the way the $100,000 is distributed, you will find that there is $70,000 for the pay of the force, $20,000 for re-arming the force and $10,000 for new buildings.

This is an increase of practically 20 per cent in the number of men. What demand has induced the government to make this increase ? I have not noticed any signs of lawlessness in the Northwest Territories that would seem to Justify it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The reason for the increase is the increase of population in the country, and the fact that we are obliged to control a larger part of the territory than formerly. For instance, instead of being able to reduce the force along the southern frontier, we shall probably have to increase it in order to protect our territories from lawlessness in the United States. Then, we have been obliged to put some detachment in the northern parts of the Territories. We have to patrol practically the whole extent of the Mackenzie river, and we intend to put a force along the shores of the Hudson Bay to protect our people from poachers, smugglers and the like. All these conditions make an increase in the force quite natural.

There is a form of quasi self-government in the Northwest Territories. Is there no other force of peace officers in the country ? Do the people depend solely and entirely on the Northwest Mounted Police ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Largely. Where municipalities have been organized there are municipal police officers, but elsewhere the protection of life and property is attended to exclusively by the mounted police.
What number is it proposed to send to the Hudson Bay territory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is impossible to say at present. We have there now Inspector Moodie and five men. We contemplate establishing three or four new posts along the coast.
Is it the practice of the mounted police to erect new buildings, or is that work done by the Public Works Department ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We erect our own buildings. The Public Works Department has nothing to do with them.

As one who has some knowledge of the conditions in the Northwest, I would take occasion to say that to-day, although the mounted police force is only half the strength it was ten years ago, there is fully ten times more work for the force to do than there was then. I think that statement will be endorsed by any one who is fairly familiar with the conditions that prevail to-day and the conditions that prevailed ten years ago. As the Prime Minister has stated, while the area of the Northwest Territories has not increased, the area patrolled by the Northwest Mounted Police has very largely increased. We are maintaining police posts on the Hudson Bay and on the Mackenzie river, and a considerable detachment is maintained north of Edmonton in the Peace river or Lake Athabasca country.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me that the immigrants going in and farming want protection, as they did when there were only a few, and Indians were roaming around ?

There are a certain number of white Canadians as well as Indians in the districts where these mounted police posts are being maintained ; and in the neighbourhood of the Mackenzie river country some of our friends the Americans are engaged in the sealing or whaler*industries.
We are sending a ship of war there, however.
Possibly we may have to do so later on, when our navy is a little better organized. But I rise chiefly to bring to the attention of the House

I want to inform the hon. gentleman that he has not answered my question. I want to know if, when people go into that country and settle down to agricultural pursuits, they requite the mounted police to protect them ? If immigration is coming in there at the rate they tell us, and I am glad to believe it is, why should the settlers want protection there any more than those in Ontario or anywhere else when they take up land?

Unquestionably there is a condition which settlement will reach in any country, in which there will be less necessity for a force of this nature, but that condition has not yet been reached in the Northwest Territories. The increase of population is not altogether in the old settled districts. As the population increases,
so does the area of settlement, and there is need to-day for police posts in dozens of localities in the Territories, which did not have, any population at all a dozen years ago.
Can you not utilize in those places the police who were in the parts that are now settled ?

There may be localities where the conditions are more nearly approaching those we have in Ontario and Manitoba and where consequently the force is not so necessary as it was some years ago, and in those parts there are very few police at present. But there has to be supervision by the police over the whole area if only for the reason that up to the present the administration in criminal matters is in the jurisdiction of this parliament. But the reason particularly why I rose is to call the attention of the government to what I consider a necessity. That is an increase in the pay of the men. However, before coming to that point I would ask the right hon. the First Minister if he has given any attention to the matter I brought forward last year regarding the pension basis. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) then found fault with my method of proceeding as not being strictly in order, on the ground that it was not competent for a private member to introduce a Fill which called for an increase in expenditure. As I explained at that time, there is a difference in the pension basis as between the officers and privates of the force, to the detriment of the latter, which should not exist. But apart from that, I believe it is necessary, for the well-being of the Northwest as well of the force, that higher pay should be given the privates.
What do they get now ?
They begin at 50 cents a day with the possibility of reaching the maximum of 75 cents a day at the end of five years. My suggestion would be that the men should be started
At 75 cents ?

At least at 60 cents a day and that the maximum of 75 cents be reached within a shorter period, say at the end of three years. Conditions are so radically changed all over Canada as regards the cost of living, there has been such a general increase in the wages of workingmen, that it is only reasonable the men of the Mounted Police force should receive higher pay than they did half a dozen years ago, and such an increase as I advocate would promote the general efficiency of the force.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman if the increase of 100 men is for the Territories alone and not for the Yukon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For the Territories alone. In the Territories the force will consist of 600 men and in the Yukon of 300 men.

I am somewhat surprised to hear the First Minister saying that a larger number of Mounted Police is necessary to-day than ten years ago. I remember quite well that, under former governments, very strong objection was made by the then opposition in the House to the number of Police in that country, but it appears now that these hon. gentlemen have come to see the error of their ways and are justifying the course of former Conservative administrations. To my mind a much smaller force would perform to-day the same service as it required a larger force to perform eight or ten years ago. The whole country is now permeated with railways.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Permeated !

Formerly when policemen were required to go to any particular section of the country from headquarters of from any particular post, they had to go on horseback, whereas to-day they can be sent east and west by rail in a very short time. Therefore, I am at a loss to understand why this increase should be called for. It would seem to indicate that we have made a mistake in bringing in the class of immigrants we are doing. Surely the people who are coming in now are not of so lawless a character that they are harder to keep under control than was the wild Indian, who was our great bugbear in days past. But the Indian population has been placed on reserves and so guarded that we have no longer to apprehend the same danger from them as we did formerly. Moreover, when we find the country more thickly settled, as it is to-day, we have less difficulty in maintaining law and order, because the population themselves may be relied on to a great extent to do that, and a much smaller force would be required than was needed some ten years ago. The hon. imember for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) pleads for higher pay for the police. I am not going to offer any objections, but I think it is high time that the stock argument of hon. gentlemen opposite to justify an increase was dropped. We were told five' or six years ago that under our new tariff and our preferential policy everything was going to be cheap. People were going to buy goods for a great deal less money. We were going to import more goods from abroad. Clothing was to come in at enormously reduced prices, and the people were going to be able to support themselves on much less money. Why, there is scarcely a week during the session but we find hon. gentlemen to your right, Mr. Chairman, pleading for increased pay for public officials on account of the Mr. CLANCY.
enormously increased cost of living. I confess that that is an argument I cannot understand. If there is any truth in the allegation that the preferential tariff has been a benefit to the people of this country, it ought to operate just the reverse way ; and, instead of the salaries growing larger they ought to grow smaller. Wre find the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) for instance, putting forth the claim for increased salaries to judges on account of increased cost of living. And the same with regard to other officials. We are told that the clothing and other things required for the Mounted Police have gone up in price notwithstanding the boasted preferential tariff which was to benefit everybody and give us the means of securing cheap clothing, cheap food, and so on.
The benefit stops -with the importer.

The benefit of the preferential tariff may not have reached the Northwest. I apprehend that it has not, and that it will take many years to do so. Why, it has not reached us in Ontario yet.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Has it not ?

We have another instance here of the government finding it necessary to change their views, just as they have found it necessary to change them on many other questions. Some of us here can remember how, in this House, hon. gentlemen opposite used to find fault with the amount of pay to the mounted police for the ardu-

ous work they were performing-much more arduous in those days than it is now.
I am not here to find fault with the increase in the numbers or with the increase in the pay, because it is well known that no finer body of men ever wore His Majesty's clothes in any country than the mounted police of Canada. In view of the splendid service they have rendered to Canada, it does not lie in the mouth of any man here, or of any man in the country, to find fault with them or to be small or mean with regard to their pay. But all this will be settled and overcome as soon as the government see fit to give that country that which it is clamouring for-the power to manage its own affairs. When they can overcome some of the little quibbles relating to school questions and other things, quibbles which should not be allowed to stand in the way of this great reform, they will see that that Northwest country should be granted provincial autonomy. When that is granted the people there will be able to govern themselves in any way they feel disposed. But so long as they are in the position they are kept in now, just so long will they be able to claim, in many places where probably they do not need it, the protection the mounted police afforded in the past. I am in accord with the hon. member who asks for higher pay. I would be willing to give them 75 cents a day. We know what inveterate smokers policemen are, and we know the spare time they have on their hands to gratify that taste. But with the increased price iu tobacco on account of the government's policy with regard to that great solace of soldier and civilian, 75 cents a day would not be out of place.
Did this government increase the duty on tobacco ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) knows what they did, and he knows the effect of it. I trust that the government, in order to stop this discussion year after year, will see fit to give us provincial autonomy in that country, and so there will be no necessity for such discussions.

It is most satisfactory that we who live in the Northwest Territories should be allowed to know exactly what is in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite in relation to this question of provincial autonomy. We have been told definitely that one' of the reasons why the opposition wishes autonomy given immediately to the people of that country is that thus upon the Northwest Territories may be thrown the responsibility of providing their own railways. And now we are told distinctly by two hon. gentlemen who occupy places on the opposition benches that the reason why autonomy should at once be granted is that the mounted police force may be immediately abolished.
Oh, oh.

I do not want to follow my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) into a tariff discussion this afternoon. To some extent he and I agree on the question of cheapness. The fact that certain things are cheap does not necessarily prove that the country is prosperous. There are things in the Northwest that, during the last six or seven years, have materially increased in price. It is in the knowledge of everybody that lands in that country have not only doubled, but quadrupled in price within the last few years. And certainly the increase in the price of lands is not to be put to the credit of a high tariff, because when we had a higher tariff than we have at present the people who owned lands in that country could not sell them in many cases at any price. We have had a discussion in recent days about cheap railways. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House said that ten-thousand-dollar-a-mile railways were wanted in that country, and that they were being built in Manitoba. The only cheap railways in the Northwest of which we have knowledge are two with which the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is connected. These cost $11,000 a mile, and at present the people of all Saskatchewan and a large portion of Assiniboia are complaining of not being able to get any facilities for" transportation over these cheap railways. The Northwest wants no more roads of this class. Let me point out to my hon. friend from Halton that, by the census of 1890 the population of the Northwest Territories amounted to 66,000 souls. At that time a very large majority of the population were of Canadian and British origin. Today, I venture to say, the population of the Northwest Territories is not less than 350,000 souls, and probably more than 50 per cent of it is not of Canadian or British origin.
What is it ?

A large proportion of it is from the continent of Europe, people whom we are glad to welcome within our borders, people who are making a great success in the work of developing our vacant lands in the Northwest Territories. But it is to the advantage of the people of the Northwest, as well as of the people of the east, that the Mounted Police should be maintained to give advice and assistance to these people. The police are needed, not so much to watch against these people's criminal proclivities, because, I venture to say, they are very 'little worse in that respect than those who come from the British islands, from the older parts of Canada, or from the United States. But together with any large movement of population there will be found a considerable element of people who do demand some attention from the civil authorities. I do not suppose we can get any better class of people than are coming from the United States. We are getting them by the tens of thousands per annum now, but amongst these

people, whom we welcome, and whose admission to the country not a man in this House would oppose for one moment, there are bound to sift in a considerable number of people whose presence makes it very advisable, to say the least, that strong police force should be maintained in that country.

Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) not giving Canada a rather bad certificate ? How will people who contemplate going into the Northwest view the statement of the hon. gentleman that they are going into a country where police protection is required because of the character of the persons who are to be their next neighbour ? Is that the certificate of character the hon. gentleman is giving our country ? The hon. gentleman should seek some other excuse, if any excuse is necessary. Of course the right hon. the Prime Minister will tell us where the 100 men are to be stationed and the duties they are to perform, but unless the increase is an increase necessary, perhaps an increase of the pay of those already in the service might be a more pressing need than the increase in number. I think that unless the hon. gentleman is persuaded that the increase in number is very much more essential to the welfare and advancement of that country than the granting to the men who have been in the service and are still in the service, a remuneration that would compare with the remuneration in other walks of life, we should grant the increase rather than increase the numbers. Speaking for myself personally, I would be willing to support additional payment, but let us first consider whether we should increase the burdens of the country unless it is absolutely necessary. We are adding 100 men to the force in the west, and if the conditions are such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) has described, and if by reason of the increase of population and the character of a considerable number of those coming in, we must add 100 to the force- for he has told us that it is not so much for protection against the Indians as to keep the settlers under the terror of the presence and existence of the Mounted Police-
I hopp the hon. gentleman will not put words in my mouth which I did not use.

I tried to give the hon. gentleman's speech the mildest interpretation I could, and I hope the hon. gentleman will feel called upon to take that all back and to find some other reason why we should have an increase of 100 men, because, otherwise, he will frighten every good citizen of every other country, who contemplates settling in our west.
I suppose the hon. gentleman from Both well (Mr. Clancy) will admit that as long as the Indians were alone in that country, there was no great neees-

sity for a mounted police force. In 1890, as I stated, we had a force of 1,000 strong, with only about 60,000 people. The movement into that country of a certain number of people made it advisable that the Mounted Police force should be organized. I believe that the hon. member for Bothwell was not in the House in 1890, but the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) was here at that time, and I do not think that he would feel it would be consistent for him to-day to oppose an increase in the Mounted Police force from 500 to 600, in view of the fact that while we have in the country to-day some 350,000 people scattered over five times the area covered in 1890, the hon. gentleman was at that time supporting the maintenance in that country, with only 66,000 people of a force twice the strength of that which wo have there to-day.

I am pleased to hear that a number t)f Americans are going into this country. We are glad to have that class of people coming in there, but you, Mr. Chairman, will remember very well the time when the Conservative government had an immigration agent in the United States and when that agent reported to the committee on agriculture that there was a movement on foot and that immigration was coming in from the United States, the friends of the hon. gentleman moved that that agent's evidence be not piinted. They said it was the most absurd proposition ever submitted to intelligent men that people from the United States would emigrate to western Canada.
What year wras that ?,

You are old enough to know without asking me that question. It was when your friends were in opposition and were talking such nonsense that they have since gone back on every principle they then submitted. It was the Conservative party who laid the foundation of the immigration from the United States and we did not think that when that part of the country became thickly populated, wTe would have to increase the police force. I would like to ask the leader oi the government if Ontario or Quebec required greater police protection as they became more thickly settled. There has been a band of Indians in my county from time immemorial, but we do not require increased protection because the country *was filling up with a peaceful settlement of industrious people. The absurd argument lias only to be stated to show' how fallacious it is. To tell me that because the country is filling in with peaceable agricultural people, they wfill require more protection. Why did not Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and the older provinces as they became thickly settled, require an increased police protection.

2698 [DOT]
So they did. The larger a city becomes, the more police it has.

No they don't. You had better read and not talk through you hat so much. Talk about Ontario requiring police protection, we never required it. The hon. gentleman says it is not so much the Indians as the siftings. 1 think there is too much Siftonism there and that is the reason they require so much protection. I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman who takes so much credit to the policy of the present government for the increased immigration, that they had nothing to do with it. The right hon. leader of the government laughs. He forgets what he and his party told us about the western country, that it was only fit for the bear and the wild Indians, and British Columbia was a sea of mountains while the Canadian Pacific Railway would never pay the grease on the axles. The speech of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) was circulated as immigration literature for the United States, and then these gentlemen have the audacity to come up here and tell us that there is greater immigration because we had higher portect-ion. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he can tell me how much lower the tariff is now than when the Conservative party was in power ?
Ask the woollen men.
No, it is not because the tariff is any lower. It is because of the preference.
What are they complaining about then ?

It is from the fact that the British manufacturers know how to manipulate and send into this country a class <if goods which is largely composed of shoddy to compete with the goods manufactured here. Other goods come from Germany, a little labour is put into them in Great Britain and then they come in here under the preferential tariff. That is because hon. gentlemen opposite made a mistake as they have made a mistake in regard to everything they have touched ever since you came into power.

The statement of the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Air. Scott) is of such a startling character that it requires some explanation. The statement that the duties of the mounted police have increased tenfold what they were ten years ago and the reason given therefore that it is due to the character of the immigration that is coming into this country are things which may be taken hold of by our friends to the south of us and may materially interfere with the settlement of our western country in the near future. The statement appearing in 1 Hansard ' that the settlers going into the Northwest are possessed of such
extraordinary criminal proclivities as to increase tenfold the duties of the mounted police within ten years is a very startling statement and one that is calculated to do serious damage to this country both as regards immigration from the United States and as regards immigration from Europe. I trust that the hon. gentleman will find some b. tt r excuse for the increase in the mounted police than that which he has been able to give to the committee.	*

What I cannot understand is that in the older settled parts of the country these police stations must be kept up the same as they were when the country was comparatively unsettled. In Wolseley, Grenfell, Areola, Estevan, Gainsborough, and even in Regina where the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) lives and where the enlightened influence of the journalistic pen which he has wielded so long, police stations are kept up. Qu'Appelle, Moosejaw, Swift Current and Medicine Hat also have their police stations. I passed through many of these places twenty-two years ago when settlement was commencing. Since then settlement has extended in every direction and the country is becoming organized. You have now an organized territory where you had a comparatively new and unsettled country before. Surely there ought to be some machinery to enforce respect for law and order in these settled portions of the country without making it absolutely necessary for the government to keep up a mounted police force and to increase it in proportion to the increase in settlement. Naturally, as civilization advances and education extends, we would expect that we would be able to dispense with the services of this force. We were told many years ago that that ought to be the natural course, but it seems that notwithstanding the rapid advance of settlement in that country it is lecessary to keep up the police force the same as it was when there were only a few Indians roaming over the plain. This seems to be a question which ought to be dealt with in some other way. There is something defective about our system, because, otherwise, we would not require to increase police force in proportion to the increase of settlement in that country.

If we had heard this statement from the hon. member for Alberta (Air. Oliver) we would not have been so much surprised, because the House is accustomed to hear that hon. gentleman abuse the character of the immigration that is going into that country. That hon. gentleman on several occasions discussed the character of the immigration that is going into the Northwest Territories and on each occasion he has seen fit to denounce a certain part of the settlers who are going in there. It was a surprise to me, at all events, to I hear the hon. member for West Assiniboia

(Mr. Scott) make suck an indictment against tke immigration that we are glad to see is flowing into the Northwest Territories. We were under the impression that that was a good class of immigration. We were under the impression from what we had heard and read and seen when we were in that country that the class of persons who were going in was a very desirable class.
The very best.

X am very glad to know from the remark made by the hon. member for West Assiniboia that he is sorry for the statements he has made and wants to withdraw them. It is never too late to repent. But it was certainly a very serious indictment which the hon. gentleman preferred against that class of people to say that the class of people whom we supposed were law-abiding citizens was such as to require a very large increase in the police force, was such that the duties devolving upon the police force were tenfold greater than they were ten years ago. I think that it is a most surprising statement that has come from that hon. gentleman. I could understand that the particular friends of the hon. member for Alberta might require some particular attention when they go on those occasional pilgrimages, but I did not suppose that that applied to the class of people coming in from the other side. The hon. member for West Assiniboia spoke particularly of those persons coming from the United States. Now when I have been in the Northwest I have had the pleasure of meeting a great many of these people from the United States and I think they are an exceptionally fine class of people.
The very best.

I am surprised and pained to know that an hon. gentleman who lives in that country, an hon. gentleman who represents a portion of that country would stand up here and say that in consequence of the' bad character of the criminal propensities
Mr. Chairman, I must protest against being so repeatedly misquoted and having my remarks so grossly and so repeatedly misconstrued.

I congratulate the hon. gentleman that even at this eleventh^ hour he sees the error of his ways and is willing to withdraw. The hon. gentleman perhaps did not appreciate the force of his language, but I appeal to hon. gentlemen who were in the committee at the time that the hon. gentleman made the statement if he did not say that it was in consequence of the criminal propensities of the settlers coming in from the other side of the line that it was necessary to increase this force. I do not believe that is so. I believe they are a very fine and law-abiding class of people. I be-

lieve they are coming into this country for the purpose of bettering themselves, for the purpose of finding homes in a country that is better governed than the country they have left behind. I believe that they have come here to support good government and X believe that if there were no policemen within one hundred miles of them they would be law-abiding citizens. I can say the same for the class of people who were there before. A good class of people have gone in there from the older parts of the Dominion, from Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to erect homes for themselves. These men have something else to do beyond following vice. They are industrious, sober, steady and they are trying to make homes for themselves and to make a nation out of those fertile plains. I do not think that this class of people requires greatei supervision than they had ten years ago. The Indians are not so dangerous as they were in the early days. They are becoming civilized, they want to drink whisky like Christians, and I do not see why the police foice should be increased on their account. But there was one remark that the hon. gentleman made with which I hardly agree, and that is that the pay of the force should be increased. I think he was too modest in his request when he said that a man on joining the force should get sixty cents a day. I believe that the first consideration should not be the number of the force but the efficiency of the force, and you cannot get first-class men unless you pay them properly. The reason for proposing to increase the force does not certainly lie in the argument of the hon. member (Mr. Scott) when he says, that the people are less law-abiding now than they were some years ago. I had same personal experience in the Northwest, and I wish to state here that I do not believe that statement.
Mr. [DOT] OLIVER. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House remind us of the old saying : None are so blind as those who will not see. One would have supposed that the knowledge which some of them obtained in the Northwest during their celebrated tour there, would have taught them that it is a country of considerable extent, and that as its population is increasing so enormously there is necessity for an increase in all public services. In a territory 800 miles in one direction and 400 miles in another, and having outposts at a distance of 2,000 miles, the question as to whether 500 men or 600 men are necessary may very well be left to those who are charged with its administration.
I wish to remind these gentlemen opposite, that it was not the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) who insinuated that the country required more policemen because of the character of the settlers; that insinuation

came from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
No.

Yes. The necessity for an increase in the number of mounted police is caused by the increase of population, and not because of a change in its character. Let us suppose that there are a quarter million people in the Territories to-day, scattered over an area of many thousands of square miles. Let me point out that in the city of Montreal, the trade centre of the Dominion, surrounded by all the appliances of civilization, with all the traditions that earry good government from one generation to another, and having a population not as large as that of the Territories, they have at present a police force of 300 men.
More.
And they want to increase the force there.

And, suppose the municipal authorities of Montreal do increase the police force, will that deter people from going to reside in Montreal or from buying property there ? Not at all. On the contrary, when it is known that the police force is to be increased in proportion to the increase of population, people will be very much more likely to take up residence and to purchase property there.
It is the same with the Northwest Territories. Within the last few years our population has increased by many thousands. That population is scattered over vastly greater areas than ever before, and there is nothing descreditable to the people of the Territories, or to the Mounted Police themselves, or to the government in the fact, that it is proposed to increase the force by 100 men. Indeed it is largely to the credit of the incoming population and of the Mounted Police and of the administration, that a larger increase in the force is not necessary. Notwithstanding that the population of Montreal is densely settled in a city, yet, if the population of Montreal had increased in the same ratio as the population of the Territories, there is no doubt that the police force of that city would be correspondingly increased. I take if for granted, that hon. gentlemen opposite are not serious, and that they are merely putting up their argument as a little joke. However, if they be serious, I would ask them to look at the conditions which prevail in the western states of Montana, Wyoming and Colorado, where the conditions as to population and the movable character of the property owned by the people are somewhat similar, and if these gentlemen compare the conditions existing In these states with the conditions existing in our Territories, I am certain they will come to the conclusion, that the Northwest Mounted Police force is one of the best investments that the Dominion of Canada ever made. I would point out also to these hon. gentlemen, that in the province of Ontario, you have not stock on the ranges which must be guarded against dishonest people who may come to any country, and that the conditions existing in Ontario are not at all comparable to those existing in the Territories.
But Montreal is similar.

The conditions in Montreal
are very dissimilar. The natural conditions in a country like the Northwest Territories render it more difficult for the police to enforce law and order than in Montreal or any other city, and it is all the more creditable to our Northwest Mounted Police that law and order are so well enforced. Let me point out further that in this fair province of Ontario where law and order have been known for generations, there have been committed within this last few years, most deplorable and most terrible murders, the perpetrators of which .have gone undiscovered and unwhipt of justice. That cannot be said of the Territories, where the rule is, that if murder is committed the murderer is discovered and punished for his crime. That is the difference in favour of the Northwest Territories, because of the presence of the Mounted Police there, as compared even with this very fair and orderly province of Ontario. I might even go so far as to suggest-and I believe it has been suggested, and very wisely suggested -that this province would do very well to adopt some such system of police as prevails in the Northwest Territories, for the protection of its innocent children from the murderer and the reprobate.

The hon. gentleman shows his absolute unfairness of argument by comparing Montreal or any other city with a rural community. There is absolutely no comparison between the two. Every one knows that it is in cities where people of vicious habits congregate, and not in rural districts.
Mr. OLIVER, Might I interrupt the hon. gentleman ? Where did these murders in in the province of Ontario, with which every one is familiar, occur-in the city or the country ?
'What murders does the hon. gentleman refer to ?

I speak of the murder near Owen Sound, which occurred last summer. I cannot think of all the cases just now, but four or five have occurred in the last few years, and one occurred the other day in the province of New Brunswick. Were these in the cities or the country ?

Murders will of course occur in the rural districts, but not to the

same extent as in the crowded cities ; and it is unfair to compare conditions in a great crowded city like Montreal with the conditions in rural communities. These provinces get along very well without any mounted police force. In the rural communities of the province of New Brunswick, the constables are used not for criminal purposes, but for the purpose of serving papers in civil actions, and they are not paid. The hon. gentleman says, compare the superior conditions in the Territories with the conditions in the eastern provinces. Does he not see that that is an argument against increasing the police force ? Why increase it if the condition of affairs there, is far superior to what it is in the city of Montreal? The hon. gentleman has defeated his own purpose. Here we have two hon. gentlemen taking opposite positions on this matter. We have the hon. member for West Assini-boia (Mr. Scott) giving as a reason why the force should be increased, the great increase of crime in the Territories consequent upon the new population, a certain portion of which was undesirable.
The hon. gentleman persists in making incorrect statements.

The hon. gentleman sees that his colleague has made a great mistake, and he is afraid that when the people read his statement, if they do read any statements of his, they will resent it and say that he is belying the country from which he comes. Consequently the hon. member for Alberta finds it necessary to give another reason, and the reason he gives is that the people of that country are more law-abiding than the people in the older provinces, and hence the mounted police force must be increased. Could absurdity further go ? I would suggest to these hon. gentlemen that in future they had better leave the defence of the estimates to the minister in charge, because when the back-benchers interfere, they only make a mess of it. These hod. gentlemen have been obstructing the estimates. These estimates would have gone through long ago if it had not been for the bumptiousness of the hon. member for West Assinibioa. He wanted to explain everything, and in order to give a reason for this increase, he had to belie the character of the people who have gone into the Northwest. Then the hon. member for Alberta was not satisfied to allow the minister to straighten the matter out, and he tried to improve on the other by saying that the reason they want the force increased is because the people are law-abiding. I would suggest to these hon. gentlemen that we shall get along with these estimates more easily, quickly and satisfactorily, if they will leave them in the hands of the responsible minister in charge and themselves keep silent.
Might I explain that the reason the country is so law-abiding is be-
cause of the presence of the mounted police force ?
That is worse and worse.

Not at all. We give credit where credit is due-just the same as Montreal is law-abiding because of the presence of the police force ; and because Toronto is law-abiding, because of the presence of its police force. Toronto is the city of churches, the city of learning, of colleges, of education, of light and knowledge generally ; but I venture to say that Toronto has a police force of several hundred men ; and I venture to say further that it cannot get along without it, and that if the police force of Toronto resigned to-morrow, good and all as that city is, there would be trouble in every street. There is no use of hon. members opposite being funny, when there is nothing to be funny about.
You are making a lot of fun.	.
Oh, no, not at all. Hon. gentlemen, of course, can laugh without anything being funny. That is a privilege they have.

The hon. gentleman, like the Russians, has been driven from one position and is now trying to seek another. The hon. gentleman gave as a reason for the increase of the mounted police force that the people were law-abiding-'that they were such a splendid class of citizens. Now the hon. gentleman tells us that they are law-abiding because of their terror of the law- that it is only by compulsion that they can be kept within bounds. I regret to find the hon. gentleman adopting the tactics of the hon. member for West Assiniboia. I really thought that he believed what he said when he said that the people of the Northwest were law-abiding and good people ; but now he gives as the only reason why they are kept in subjection, and the only reason why murder and rape and all other vices are not rampant in the country is that they are kept in order by the mounted police ; and therefore, in order to prevent these crimes increasing, the force must be increased.

Mr. Chairman, I object to the hon. member or any one else putting words into my mouth which I did not use.
I am responsible for what I say, and if the hon. member cannot find in what I say, cause for comment or argument, I ask your protection against words being imputed to me which I did not use, and ideas which I did not express.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that if a statement is charged against an hon. gentleman, and he denies having made such a statement, that must end the matter fully and completely there and then.

I have not violated that or any other rule of this House. I am not

in the habit of violating any of the rules of the House. X said that was the only inference from the hon. gentleman's statement. I say now that the only fair inference to be drawn from the hon. gentleman's words is that it is necessary to increase this force in. order that the population in the Territories may be kept law-abiding.
The hon. gentleman has stated repeatedly that I used certain language. I did not use the words he charges me with having uttered, and I ask, Sir, for your protection.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is in order provided the hon. member who had the floor sat down.
I sat down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is right. The hon. gentleman sat down and the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) was consequently perfectly in order.

I did not know that we were discussing that particular point. The hon. gentleman has asked for additional protection. He is so used to ask for police protection in that country that he is asking for protection in this House. I had no intention of assaulting the hon. gentleman by words or in any way. On the contrary,
I am a very peaceful citizen.

I have no objection to the hon. gentleman drawing any inference he pleases so long as he calls it an inference, but I must ask you, Mr. Chairman, to protect me against having language imputed to me which I did not use. The hon. gentleman is welcome to whatever inferences he chooses to draw, but when he charges me with using certain language, he must confine himself to the facts.

Do not go too fax'. The people would only laugh at you if you made such a statement out there.
Mi-. FOWLER. If they were all like the hon. gentleman, I would not like to give them such a good character. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) may not be so law-abiding, but I am speaking of the general character of the people. They are a class of people whom I admire very much, and I very much dislike hearing them in any way reviled or vilified. I trust now the estimate will pass.

The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) gave as a justification for this increase in the number of the Northwest Mounted Police, the increase in population. He said that whereas in 1890 there were only 60,000 people in that country, to-day there were over 350,000, and it was consequently necessary to have an additional number of police to keep peace.
At that time we had a thousand men.

The province of Manitoba has doubled her population and does not ask for any Northwest Mounted Police to preserve law and oi-der. One of two things must be wrong. Either these hon. gentlemen are wrong in the conclusion they draw or you would have a different condition of things in Manitoba. We used to have the argument before from hon. gentlemen opposite that if that country were properly governed fx-om Ottawa, thei-e would be no insurrections or rebellions and no need for Mounted Police at all. But to-day, although the people have been during the last seven or eight years enjoying what hon. gentlemen opposite would call good government-
Hear, hear.

What the hon. gentleman said was that the people of the Noi-thwest were peaceful because of the pi-esence of the Mounted Police. What inference could I draw from that except that the reverse would be the case were it not for that body ?
I did not say anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That must end the niatter.

It cannot prevent my drawing an inference from the hon. gentleman's language. I say that his language was such as to lead us to the conclusion that the people of the Northwest Territories were only peaceful and law-abiding because of the presence of the Mounted Police. I resent that imputation on behalf of the people of the Territories, and I assert that the people of the Northwest Tex;ritoi-ies would be peaceful- and law-abiding even if thei-e were no Mounted Police within a hundred miles of them.
Mi-. SPROULE-they say it is absolutely necessary, in the interests of peace and order, to increase that force twenty per cent. In this advancing stage of civilization, in which the press of the country is doing civilizing work, aided so effectively by the hon. gentlemen from Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) and Alberta (Mr. Oliver), in which schools are being established and educational facilities greatly extended, and in which the government of the country is in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite, are we to be told that our civilization is a failure and an increase in the Mounted Police force an absolute necessity ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentlemaxi were to submit to the people of the. Northwest Territories the proposition that they should be given pi-ovincial autonomy conditional on the Northwest Mounted Police force being abolished, he would not find in the Territories five hundred people out of the four hundred thousand to vote in favour of his proposition.
Give them a chance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the people were to understand that the abolition of this force, and consequently our present system of maintaining law and order in that vast country, should follow the granting of provincial autonomy, there would be no popular support whatever to that proposition. So far as the proposed increase is concerned, a moment's consideration of the conditions during the past seven or eight years will illustrate very clearly the difficulties under which the management of the force have laboured. When the change of government took place in 1896, the white population of the Territories was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100,000. At that time the Yukon Territory occupied only the attention of some nineteen or twenty mounted policemen. There was a small force at Fort Cudahy. Immediately after 1896, the opening up of the Yukon country necessitated drawing from the force of some 250 or 300 men for service in that country, and it was necessary to draft the most seasoned, experienced and capable men. Any one who knows anything of the ordinary constitution of a police force of 500 or 600 men will know that if you take away from that force 250 or 300 of its best men, you will have a body which it is very difficult to operate efficiently. Then came the fact that owing to the assiduous nature of the duties in the Yukon, many of the men who were sent out to that country left the force altogether upon the earliest opportunity. Following that again came the drain upon the force which resulted from the call to arms in South Africa. The result of all this has been that the original force, ns it stood in 1896, of trained and disciplined men. was so impaired in quality, that it became extremely difficult for the commanding officer to maintain it in that efficiency which it is desirable a force of that kind should possess. At present, looking to the facts that 300 men have to be maintained in the Yukon, that the number of outposts throughout the Territories has largely increased, and that trained and disciplined men have been largely taken away for the reasons I have given, it will toe seen that the position taken by the management of the force that they require an additional number in order that they may be able to keep a larger number at headquarters than they can at present, is amply justified.
Now, one of the great difficulties which the commanding officer in the mounted po lice meets with in the operations of his force is that the men pass out at the end of their time. Many of the best men are taken off to the Yukon Territory. The tendency is such that, in what we ordinarily call the Northwest Territories, the green men of the force are left. It is perfectly well known to men of experience in connection with a force of this kind that it takes at least two years before a man can be sufficiently Mr. SIFTON.
trained to be sent out to an isolated post where he must depend upon his own resources. He ought to be a year and a half or two years in the force before he is sent to occupy such a position. But, under present circumstances, it is impossible to carry out that principle. My recollection of my last conversation with the comptroller is that he said it is difficult for him to keep a man even six months on the force before he must be sent to duty of an isolated character. Some of the slips that have taken place in connection with the administration of justice-I am glad to say they have been rectified by increased diligence later-were due to the fact that the comptroller was in such a position that he was forced to employ men in outpost duty whom he knew to be not properly fitted for such duty. But they were the only men he had. One of the great points to be gained by the increase is that the comptroller may have a larger measure of power to keep men at headquarters under instruction and discipline, so that when they are sent out to outpost or isolated duty they will be so trained and posted in regard to their duties and will have had such experience that the country can depend upon the duty entrusted to them being properly performed.
Now, a word in regard to the general features of this case. I am not going to talk of the province of Ontario, the province of ,New Brunswick, or any of the eastern provinces. This government is not responsible for the administration of criminal justice in these provinces, and so it is a matter with which, at the present time, we are not concerned. But in the province of Manitoba, where, perhaps, some argument might be drawn, there is the large city of Winnipeg, where there is a permanent military depot and an efficient militia force which can be called upon at any time, and has been called upon from time to time for the purpose of suppressing civil disorder. That furnishes a foundation for the establishment of law and order which does not exist up to the present time in the Northwest Territories. The existence of that military depot, with the permanent force that can be called upon is of strong assistance to the civil power. But. apart from that, the fact that we have in the Northwest Territories a country of vast expanse, where, only a short time ago, the Indians were not in a satisfactory state of subjection, and where, it has been learned by experience, outbreaks were not impossible, makes it of the utmost importance- especially now, when we have, after enormous expenditure, turned the tide of population into that territory-that no indications should be given of a tendency to reduce in any way the practical efficiency of the mounted police. One of the things which attracts to our Northwest, settlers from the United States-settlers of the most valuable character-the argument which draws them with the greatest power, is the fact that we

have in this force of mounted police a system of administering justice, of preventing crime and punishing crime, that is the admiration of and the envy of the western states of the union. Especially at this time, it seems to me, it is of the utmost importance that no paltry consideration of economy in connection with this service should prevent us from keeping the force up to a point of as great efficiency, or even greater efficiency, than in. the past. The people of Canada, without respect to parties, are proud of the mounted police. We do not expect perfection in anything human, but the mounted police has been as nearly perfect in assisting the administration of justice as it was possible for any force to be. The purpose of the Prime Minister in making the recommendation is not to allow of indulgence in useless extravagance, but to strengthen this arm of the service so necessary at the present time. So far as I am concerned, I may say that, five years ago. before the drain upon the force had taken place in connection with the Yukon 'Territory and, later on, in connection with the force for service in South Africa, I was in favour of curtailing expenditure on the mounted police as far as possible. But in view of the fact that the scope of activity of the force was so increased, it is of the utmost importance that no impression should prevail, or be allowed to prevail, that we have any intention of weakening the force or abandoning the system by which we have hitherto attained such magnificent results in the maintenance of order in the Northwest Territories. It seems to me that the committee ought to be absolutely unanimous in strengthening the hands of the government to carry this into effect. I was not in my place when this debate began. But if hor.. gentlemen opposite have shown any desire to oppose this proposition, I think that upon full and fair consideration of the whole matter they will see that, if they were in the Vsame position as the government^ they would make the same proposals as we are making, and would be entitled to the support of their opponents in doing so.

The closing remark of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) is a good reason why we should not criticise the statement he has made. He was not in the House when the discussion commenced, and, consequently, a great deal of what he said, while exceedingly interesting, is not apposite to the discussion which took place prior to his entry. If he had been present he would know that the discussion was due to the language used by some hon. gentlemen on that side with reference to the character of the immigration now going into the Northwest. They explained that because of the increase of undesirable people there must be an increase in the Mounted Police force. That it was that gave rise to the discussion that has been going on for more than an hour. But, as it went on, conflicting rea-861
sons were given by hon. gentlemen opposite lor the increase in the force. There was no objection to that increase, so far as I have heard, from hon. gentlemen on this side. On the contrary, there has been an upholding of the hands of the government, not only in the increase of the force, but in the increase of the pay. I, for one, would be glad to support a proposition to give the police a larger increase of pay than has been recommended by gentlemen on the treasury benches. Now, as to the reasons that have prompted the increase in the force, one given by the Minister of the Interior was the increased immigration from the United States. I am sure we can congratulate the Minister of the Interior upon the statement he has made with respect to this matter. The record which the Mounted Police has made is a creditable record, and those who established that force, and those who maintained that force in the Northwest Territories in the face of very strenuous opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite, are those who are entitled to credit for the reputation that force has made for the country, and for the peace and security that settlers in that country have enjoyed by reason of the magni-ficient work the force has done. I cordially support .the proposition made by hon. gentlemen opposite to increase the pay and increase the number of men.

Who established the force ?
Mi-. CLARKE. I say that those who established it are entitled to the credit for the good name the country has gained through the work of the force. I would ask if there are special districts where it is intended to increase the number of men-any particular posts ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it is not the intention to locate this additional force of 100 men in any particular place, I may say that the intention is to have a larger number at Regina to train the men there. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) a moment ago, suggested that there was no necessity for the depot at Regina. The depot we have there is not for the purpose of protecting the town so much as it is a drilling depot. We intend to keep a large number of men there to be drilled. And we intend to keep a large number of men there for drilling, because as has been stated a moment ago by the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) the force has been very much drawn upon for the South African war and different causes, and now while we have a splendid force, we believe that it can be made still more effective if we can keep the men longer at the head depot.

I would not wish the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) to misunderstand the position taken by the opposition this afternoon. I understood the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott)

to give as one of the reasons for increasing the force that there was a certain lawless element coming into the Northwest Territories. If I am wrong in that statement I will be very glad to allow the hon. gentleman to correct me.
Make your speech.
Then I am correct.

Let my hon. friend not further misrepresent me. I did not say he was correct. I advised him to go on and make his statement. There is, however, an element of truth in the statement he attributes to me. What I said was that in any large movement of population-and we have in recent years been receiving tens of thousands of good people, the best class that could be got to come into this territory from the Western States-there is bound to be a certain proportion of lawless element come along with the greater number of better class people.
That is to say there is a certain element of undesirable people coming into the Northwest Territories.
Yes, a very small proportion I am pleased to say, but a proportion.

Now that we have arrived at this correction where is the difference between the statement of the hon. gentleman and the ground we have taken on this occasion ? We have simply charged that the hon. gentleman made that statement and he did not like the statement he had made. I have heard several reasons this afternoon why this item is increased, but I am bound to say the hon. gentlemen opposite have not given all the reasons for the increase.
They have not been half stated.

They have not been half stated. Well we have taken up a good deal of time discussing matters not pertaining to this question it would perhaps become hon. gentlemen from that district to give us the reasons why we are increasing that item. I find in the commissioner's report that he uses this language
The rapid settlement of a new country always attracts a certain lawless and undesirable element, and it is evident, from the year's crime reports, that the Northwest Territories are not an -exception.
The settlement of the Territories will probably increase at the rate of at least 100,000 a year for several years to come. It is among these that the unrecorded and often unrecognized, work of the force will he most valuable.
The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific will call for large numbers of labourers. It is well known that the rapid construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was considerably facilitated by the maintenance of order among the army of navvies.
The .Grand Trunk Pacific will require like assistance, and will be benefited in the same way. 1 Mr. INGRAM.
That is borne out by an officer of the government. Now here is one of the chief items why this increased item is asked.
Perhaps I would not be going too far if I said that that would not be a sufficient reason this year to ask a vote for increased Mounted Police for I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House will say that the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific will take place in the present year in this-district.
What about the Canadian Northern ?
I am referring only to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Does the hon. gentleman intend to obstruct all summer ?

I may say to the horn member for Alberta that I am stating what is pertinent to the question, but he did not.
I have no objection to an increase of pay to the Mounted Police force, and I might go as far as to say that I believe if instead of . increasing the number we would increase the pay of the 500 men we now have, it would probably be more in the interest of the Mounted Police force. In Manitoba, for some years, we had Mounted Police, but as settlement came in and the district became better filled up there was less reason for having Mounted Police and as a result the police were removed from Manitoba. Perhaps it would be in the interest of the people of the Northwest Territories as well as of the force that the establishment at Regina might be greatly reduced and distributed in the newer sections where it might be really necessary to have the Mounted Police stationed. I am glad to see that although we might expect to see more or less smuggling along the boundary line, if I am to be guided by this report, there was not in 1903 and 1902 a single crime against the Customs law in the Northwest Territories. That is something of which we must be very proud, but I find that a certain class of crimes has greatly increased in the Northwest Territories, that is crimes in respect of religion and morals. Many of us know that certain things have occurred there that may be a great crime against religion and morals, but I for one would not pretent to say that the same thing might occur another year and probably it will not occur for many years to come. 1 wish my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) to understand that I am willing to support any reasonable expenditure that will bring about any good for the Northwest Territories, and I believe that is the view of every gentleman on this side of the House.
I would at the same time ask, in view of the large increase in population in the Northwest Territories from 100,000 in 1S9G to 350,000 or 400,000 to-day, why these people with nearly one half million of population should be deprived of provincial

autonomy ? Why should they not have the right to govern themselves, and to administer justice in their territories or provinces the same as the other portions of this country ? Surely it cannot be said that we, the Parliament of Canada, are better qualified to administer the affairs of the Northwest Territories than representatives of the people elected directly for that purpose in their own territories or provinces would be. 1 think the right hon. gentleman is neglecting this portion of the Dominion when he refuses to grant provincial autonomy to the people of the Northwest Territories.
Subsistence, light, fuel, clothing &c., $270,000.
There is an increase here of $67,000. Is this in a fair proportion to the increase in the number or is it to increase the pay of the present force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is not with a view of increasing the pay of the men now on the force. The question of increased pay is under consideration at the present time, and we may have to ask parliament for a further appropriation under this head. The increase of $100,000 is for the pay of the men at the in'esent time, for the re-arming of the force and for new buildings and repairs.
Where do you propose to put up the new buildings ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not contemplated to erect any new buildings anywhere but simply to repair the buildings wherever they are.
Yukon Territory

pay of force	$170,000
Subsistence, forage, fuel and light clothing, repairs and renewals, horses, dogs, arms and ammunition, medical stores, stationery, billeting, transport and contingencies	 320,000
Buildings	 25,000

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is exactly the same vote as last year with the exception of $15,000 of an increase which is for the re-arming of the force.
How many men do you keep in the Yukon ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: The same as the first ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. We increased the force by fifty men two or three years ago when we were threatened with an invasion, and we have kept them there.

I understood that the reason for the increase at that time was that there were signs of trouble across the line and that these men must be required only for a short time after which the government might be able to reduce the number. Does the same reason exist still ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. I am happy to say that the territory is very quiet and orderly and that there are no threats of a character similar to that which we had a few years ago. We are obliged to keep the present force up to the strength of 300 because we are always asked to establish new posts in the course of the development of the country. When new discoveries are made and when there is a rush of miners to these places we have to follow them so as to preserve law and order. We have more posts to maintain and I am afraid we will have to keep adding to them all the time.
Are the Mounted Police there used as collectors of customs, or do they do other work ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They assist all the departments, customs, the excise, the agriculture, and the quarantine. If anything arises which is not in the ordinary run of business the force is called upon to render service.
The right hon. gentleman says that he is re-arming the police. They were armed with the Lee-Enfield carbine. What new arm are you going to give them ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have only 200 Lee-Enfield rifles. They are to be rearmed with the Ross rifle.
You are getting a further supply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are replacing the old supply.

Before we leave this item, may I ask my right hon. friend the leader of the government, if he recollects the proposition that was made last year by myself in the form of a Bill in regard to pensions for the privates of the force and whether it would not be possible at this session to change the Act in the direction suggested last year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The matter is under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will take up the civil government vote of the Department of Inland Revenue, page 10.

I understood from the hon. leader of the opposition, who is not present now, that he had been notified that we would take up the right hon. Prime Minister's estimates and then the estimates of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. We are prepared to discuss the estimates of the hon. Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is right. I informed him that we would take up my own, those of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and those of the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We are prepared to go on with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought the Department of Inland Revenue was included in that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No.
I would be perfectly willing to go on with any department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood, but the Prime Minister understood otherwise, that Inland Revenue was included.

The message that came to me was that the Prime Minister's estimates and the estimates of the Department of Agriculture would be taken up, and I communicated with the whips, who informed the members accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And also Marine and Fisheries.

That may have been lost in the process of transmission to me.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER. At all events,
I intended to say that Agriculture and also Marine and Fisheries would be taken up.
I did not hear anything about Marine and Fisheries, but of course as I say, it may have been lost in transmission.

Very well, we will call it six o'clock.
