There is an increase over last year of about $2,000, which is due chiefly to the statutory increases and to some increases resulting from the changes made in 1 Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the Civil Service Act last year, requiring that certain clerks at the limit of their classes under the old law should receive increases, the limit of their classes having been raised. It is also due to the fact that Messrs. Kilgallin and Bourret were formerly paid out of the vote for the classification of patents, a work which had been going on for five or six years ; but as that work is now being done along with other work in the department-by these two men, the special vote for it is not taken this year, and they are now put on the regular permanent list of the department. They passed the civil service examination, but as they are past the age for entering the service, the Act requires that they shall be named, and therefore their names appear in this item.
I understand that last year there were 55 clerks while now there are 59, so that there are four additional ?

Yes, two of these are the gentlemen I have just mentioned, and the two others are second-class clerks who have come from the Secretary of State's department in consequence of the transference to my department of records which are to be joined to the archives. As these two clerks are on the list of my department, their names and the appropriations for them will be dropped from the estimates of the Secretary of State's Department.
Has the appointment of archivist been made yet ?
Yes, Mr. A. G. Doughty, of Quebec, has been appointed.

How is it that you start these two clerks at $800 a year ?
Mr. FISHER, That is the salary they were getting as temporary clerks, and the Act provides that they may come in at the same salary.
Mi-. SPROULE. My understanding of the Act is that it provides that a temporary clerk cannot go above a certain figure.
They were not temporary clerks under the Civil Service Act, but under the vote for the classification of patents, to which the Civil Service Act did not apply.
When did they pass the Civil Service examination ?

Mr. Kilgallin entered the service in 1890 as an extra clerk and Mr. Bourret in 1884. Their salaries were raised from time to time until they reached the figure here mentioned, and under the Act passed last session they come into the service at the salaries they were receiving. Mr. Kilgallin passed the Civil Service examination in 1896 and Mr. Bourret in 1889-
How many permanent and temporary clerks were there in 1896 and how-many now ?
1 could not off hand^give the numbers. Roughly speaking, the number is about the same of temporary and permanent clerks.
The same proportion ?

About the same. I cannot remember the exact number. A few years ago there was considerable reduction, but in consequence of the expansion of the patent office and the work of classification the number was somewhat increased.
Would the hon. gentleman give the figures before he is through with his estimates ?
Certainly.
Are there any other clerks in the department who have not passed the civil service examination ?

I do not think so. There are none in the inside service who have not either passed the examination or been admitted by special vote. There may be some who were admitted by special vote as in the present instance.
Cbntingencies, including M. Foley at $500, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $18,750.
Why do you have this ?

, Foley was a messenger and worked at tile classification of patents. He has not passed any qualifying or preliminary examination, and consequently I have to* insert these words. He is an efficient man who has been doing the work of the department for several years, and it would be unjust to turn him out.
Have messengers to pass the civil service examination ?
They have to pass a preliminary examination.

When is this sort of pro-riiotion going to cease ? Does the hon. minister think it is fair to the large number of men who are passing civil service examinations every year, that every session there should be a large number of officials legislated into these positions who have not passed any examination ?

It would not be fair to take a man from the outside unless he had passed the examination, but when a man has been in the service for years doing good work, it would be unfair to dismiss him when there is still plenty of work to be done for which he is thoroughly competent.
Then you will never reach the point when a man will be unable to get into a department without passing the civil service examination ?

These officials are taken into the different departments from year to year to do work for which no special qualification
is required and no civil service examination necessary. After they have been employed by the government some years and have given every evidence of their efficiency, it would not be fair to dismiss them when there is still plenty of work for them to do, which they are well able to perform. Mr. Foley is too old to pass an examination now, so that even if he did pass it. these words would require to be inserted, because he is beyond the age limit provided in the Act. When he was brought in to do the classification of patent work, he was brought in practically as a labourer. He handled all the old patents, of which there were some 70,000 or 80,000, which had to be taken down and dusted and brought to the men who did the work Of classification and then put them back in their places. He has done that work all along-purely labourer's work, which does not require any special qualification. but only neatness and industry. He will still go on doing that work as it is required, but as we have caught up with the arrears, I have done away with the vote for that classification, and am asking to have Mr. Foley put on permanently as messenger.
How will he stand with regard to superannuation ?
He will come in under the new Act.
But these men have not passed any examination.
Mr. Foley is the only one who has not passed.
And what position do the others occupy with regard to superannuation ?
When these items were passed these gentlemen will contribute under the present Retiring Allowance Act- that is, five per cent of their income will be retained towards the retiring allowance.
That is the same as with others ?
Yes. But Mr. Foley would not contribute, because he is paid out of contingencies as a temporary employee. He does not become a permanent employee even when this is passed.
When will the superannuation period of the others count from from the time they come in ?
The retention of five per cent of their salaries begins from the time they become civil servants, and when this goes through they become members of the civil service.
It would not be retroactive ?
No. Because they were not members of the civil, service but were employees under different footings.

These men. I understood, were taking down and classifying the patents. What X cannot understand is the justification for incurring such an expense when it was contemplated, and afterwards carried out, to sell these models and sell them for a mere trifle.
The hon. gentleman (Hr. Sproule) does not understand the difference between the patent records and the models.
I think I do.

The models have nothing to do with the application. When an application is made for a patent, it is referred to the examiner, whose duty it is to find out if the invention has already been patented in Canada or elsewhere. To do this he must consult the records in the patent office. Before this classification work was undertaken, they were in sequence bv numbers and a dozen totally different kinds of patents might succeed one another-generally did. The classification was an arrangement into classes and sub-classes so that the examiner could refer at once to patents of a similar character to one sought by the applicant, instead of having to search through all the patents, as was formerly the case. It was almost impossible, formerly, to carry out the search, but now it is comparatively easy.

I still think it was not the part of wisdom to sell out the models. The classification of patents is as desirable for the future as for the past. The advantage was this-and I speak from some experience-
Does the hon. gentleman speak of the classification ?

I am speaking of the classification, and the unwisdom of selling the models. For instance, I send the patent records to an individual and he selects a patent that he thinks would be useful for his purposes. He sends an agent or comes to Ottawa, as has been done within my knowledge, to look at the model and gain such information as he thinks necessary. On the basis* of that information, he may make an arrangement with the patentee with regard to the invention. But now, if such a party comes here to examine a model, he finds that the models have been sold. I understand that the models were sold for $800. I thought at the time it was the greatest piece of folly I had ever heard of, and I think so still.

For thirteen years models have not been required of those asking for patents. My predecessors in office decreed that models should not be required, but only a drawing and description. This is still the law. A patent is given for eighteen years, and when the models were required the patent only covered fifteen years, so that many of the models were of'inventions the patents on which had expired. The draw-

ings are the things that we have been classifying, and reference to the drawings is very much easier in such cases as those the hon. gentleman cites of parties coming here to gain information with regard to patented inventions. Before the classification, the party would have to search through the whole patent records or the patents themselves, and it was like searching for a needle in a bundle of hay. I think that less than two years of the models were those of patents that had not expired. For some five years most of the models had been packed away in boxes and not accessible to the public.
They were down in a room on Sparks street.

It is a year and a half since they were removed from there, and. at best there were very few in that place-I should think not more than ten per cent of them. Some of them, I found when I came into office, were packed away in boxes in an old building at the mouth of the canal. Many of them were in the roof of the Langevin block, and some in the cellar in a building on Sparks street. We were incurring constant expense renting places in which to store them, and they were of no use, because they were not accessible. And over fifty per cent were models of patents which had expired. Under the circumstances, it seemed not worth while to go on caring for them, and so I took power to dispose of them. The classification, however, has nothing to do with the models, because it is a classification of the drawings, which are all there and arranged in such a way as to be easily accessible.
I thought the minister said that the work these men were doing was taking down these models and classifying them ?
No, but taking down the files.
Does it take three men to take down the files ?

No-one man. But it took three men to do this work of classification. There are over 70,000 patents. These are the actual patents, folded up with the record of tiie application, the drawings, &c. in the file, and put in place. We have tiers and tiers of them in the room in the patent office. These had all to be taken down and examined by the gentleman who was classifying them so as to decide in what class they should go. The drawings were taken out of the file and put in the classes to which they belonged, so that they can be examined by the public or the examiners.
Was there no system of classification before ?
Not the slightest.

There must be something wrong about that because I know in presenting applications to the department the information given me was that they required a certain length of time to examine the patents already in existence and to see whether the patent applied for infringed upon any rights or if the invention was patentable. If they were thrown together in a haphazard way I do not see how this search could be made in so short a time.

I can assure my hon. friend that what I have said was exactly correct. The patents were all there in consecutive order, not in any way classified, and the consecutive numbers of patents had no reference to the thing for which the patent was given. But there were the indices to the pateut record, simply the name and nothing else. The examiners would refer first to that ; they might get a hint from the index or they might not. That was the case when I asked for money to classify the patents ; I made that request on the initiative of the officers of the department who explained the situation to me aud it seemed to me almost as wonderful as to my hon. friend that they had not been classified long ago.
Had these officers any special qualifications to classify the patents?

The gentleman who had charge of the classification is Mr. Caron, one of the oldest examiners in the office. These gentlemen were simply his assistants who were under him and assisted him in the routine work.

As I understand it, special examiners would be designated to examine special classes of patents of which they would have special knowledge, and therefore would be capable of judging. In classifying all the patents that would be a very serious undertaking for those making applications for patents. For instance it might be that a patent would be granted to some one for an article which had already been patented and which he would find infringed on some other patent with the result that he would be spending money on a useless patent and perhaps become involved in a law suit.

I quite agree and that is why I asked for power to have a classification made. Mr. Caron who is doing the work is an old employee in the department thoroughly competent. He spent some time with the late deputy Mr. Scarth, in working out the system on which they would arrange the classification, and they went to Washington to examine the classification there. They made a special arrangement with the Washington authorities that they would exchange with us their classification for our classification. After a while, however, they ceased to send us their classification and
when I remonstrated, they said they could not continue because they found it too onerous. My hon. friend thinks that this work may not have been done efficiently ; I believe it was done efficiently, but at the same time we have this guarantee that the present examiners are constantly referring to it. Every time a question conies up, they go to the classification and if they should find anything wrongly placed they would recognize that and immediately correct the error. Mr. Kilgallin is the man especially in charge of this and having been engaged in the classification knows exactly where to put his hand on any particular class or subclass. It is he who gets the classes and sub-classes for the examiners, and if any of them found in a class a drawing that was not correctly placed they would immediately refer it to him and he would examine and see where it should be. That is the only check we have, but we have not found that check necessary to any great extent.
Am I right in tinderstanding that it is not necessary to deposit a model in the department and has not been necessary for the past thirteen years ?
It is not required but we have the right to demand a model.
I had to deposit a model.
My hon. friend need not have done so.
I did not do it for fun.
I said the department had a right to demand one.
I understood you to say that it is not necessary and has not been for thirteen years.

When an application comes in the applicant does not have to send in a model with his application as he did until thirteen years ago. If, after the application comes in, the examiner finds himself in such difficulties that he requires a model, he can ask the applicant for one, but it is very rarely required.
I think the minister is right in respect to that; it is very rarely asked for and in any case the plans and specifications serve all the purposes of a model.
I was informed through a firm of solicitors here that a model was required.
That is incorrect.
Is this classification merely an indexing ?

No, the patents have been divided into large classes and then these classes have been subdivided into smaller

classes. I will give an illustration. We may, for instance, take all the classes of agricultural implements. Then, there might be a class such as drills. There might be another class such as cultivating machinery, or threshing machines. I am merely illustrating. I do not know whether this is the case or not, but this is the kind of thing. These classes have been worked out by the gentleman who is in charge of this classification. He worked the classifications out after carefully examining the Washington classification which was done before ours. Then, he takes the patents in the order of their numbers. For instance, he sees that a patent belongs to such and such a class and to such and such a sub-class. He does not have the patent there but it is represented by a drawing bearing the number of the patent. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the drawing is what the examiner wants, when an application for a new patent is made so as to ascertain if there is a patent in force covering the invention in respect of which the application is made. The classification is going on. The drawings as sent in originally were unsatisfactory, many of them being old and a great many of them not very correct. And when the classifications were prepared two cardboard drawings-drawings on stiff cardboards of a particular shape and size-were put into the class very much like the card index system which a great many people are familiar with in library work.
How many years ago did this classification commence, and what amount of money has been expended on it ?
In 1899 the work was commenced.
How much has been expended to date ?
I would have to look back into the estimates. One year $5,000 was spent, another year $4,000 and another year $3,000
Are we to understand that it is completed now ?
It is completed up to date. We have about 5,000 or 6,000 applications a year and these have to be classified as they come in.
The classification will go on ?
Yes, this is what Mr. Kil-gallin has on hand.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if this amount is required altogether for the classification of these patents or if any part of it will be used for the benefit of the farmer ?

This is the inside service of the department. A good deal of the work that is done for the benefit of the Mr. FISHER.
farmer is done by the outside service. The experimental farms do not come under this vote at all, the commissioner of agriculture and dairying does not come under this, the veterinary branch does not come under this, the quarantine branch does not come under this. This is simply for the inside service of the department which has to deal with patents trade marks, copyright, archives, statistics and so on.
A few days ago I asked the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) a question in regard to assisting the farmers in their operations in this country as follows :

1.	Is the intention of the government to reduce railway rates to a nominal figure, or admit of free passes, for agricultural delegates over public railways, in accordance with the resolution passed at the annual convention of the Prince Edward Island farmers ?
2.	What is the lowest existant rate paid by delegates attending such conventions, and the fares, when formally engaged in promoting the public interests, and thus increasing railway traffic ?
3.	Should not those gentlemen giving their time and brains to the advancement of the country, be provided with free transportation ?
The hon. Minister of Railways of Canals, whom I do not see in his place this evening, made this reply :

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
I cannot very well understand whether this question relates to railways generally or merely to the government railway. I may say further that the deputy minister informs me that no trace of any such resolution as that referred to in the first question can be found in the department. The second question relates to special rates on railways generally throughout Canada. That information is not in the department. The third question involves the free transportation on the government railw-ays of all those who devote their time and brains to the advancement of the country. Our rolling stock might not he sufficient to convey all of these.
I looked upon it that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was treating the farmers of this country in a very light way. When I said public railways I meant government railways. The public railway is a railway owned by the government. A corporation railway is a railway owned by a company. I would have supposed that that hon. gentleman would have given me an answer more in accordance with the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am afraid I must draw the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) to the fact that this is not relevant to the question under discussion. I think the hon. gentleman might bring that up at some future time when

another point will come up, but I think it will be a waste of time to discuss that question at the present time. X hope the hon. gentleman will look upon it in that way and allow it to stand until an opportunity presents itself to again bring the matter up. The danger of taking up a question that is outside of the question being considered is that the discussion may take a wide range and it is very difficult to keep it down to the question under consideration. I would ask the hon. gentleman to defer the discussion of this question until the proper time.

I will obey your orders, Mr. Chairman, but I would like to bring to the notice of this committee in connection with these contingencies the fact that something should be done for the farmers of the country more than has been done of late. I was led to ask this question because of a letter appearing in the ' Maritime Farmer,' a paper published in Sussex, N.B. This is strictly in connection with the subject of contingencies in regard to the farmers of this country. My question was based on the following extract. Am I in order, Mr. Chairman V

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afriad the hon. gentleman is wandering outside of the item of contingencies in reference to this special department, but I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman will have opportunities in abundance to bring up the question and discuss it fully in perfect order. I would ask him to allow this item to pass and probably in a little while we will come to an item in which he can discuss it in order and thus facilitate the business at the present time.

I submit to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but at the same time I desire to ask what part of the expenditures on these contingencies is for the farmers of the country and I desire also to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture to use his influence with the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in the endeavour to persuade him to do something in connection with bettering the condition of the farmers. It will only tafce a moment for me to read this letter of the Rev. Alfred Edward Burke writing to the editor of this paper, the ' Maritime Farmer.' He says :
We contended at the late convention, with a unanimous House behind us, that special treatment would have to he meted out to the agricultural conventions of the country, which are more effectually doing the work of national development than all the other innumerable divisions of the body politic. Just imagine you and me and so many others giving our time, brain and best effort to the furtherance of these farming ends on which the community depends, and the railroads over which we are formally engaged in making traffic, treating us and our conventions in the same calculating way as any other assembly of men convened for
purely personal or corporate concerns ! We have to pay the same fares, subscribe to the same restricting conditions as these, and then put our hands into our pockets again and discharge the hotel bills and other incidentals to travel, while we are on purely public business. This is manifestly unfair and unjust and must stop. We contend that the cost of travel by public roads to conventions such as ours should never have been more than merely nominal and now should be wiped out altogether in the best interests of the community.
Dealing with officials, we are met with the precedent bugaboo, the precedent borrowed from private corporations ; evidently, we must bring our demands to the doors of parliament. Personally, we can say that on many occasions corporate roads have not only furnished us with free transportation but also paid travelling expenses and compensated to some extent at least for time and effort expended in work -which only indirectly affected them, whilst the country received population and trade ; now the people's own roads take our time and effort and tax us as highly as any other for the travelling we are compelled to do in the general interest; indeed specially narrow considerations have of late entered into the local conduct of thedej matters which, for the sake of common decency must speedily be remedied. It were indeed time that the people knew their rights in these matters ; and, knowing, dare defend. Our association in common with others of a like nature, then, is asking for special treatment and we will not let up either until it is conceded.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must insist that this discussion shall cease now.
By your favour. Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the Minister of Agriculture if the farmers of this country should not have a share of these contingencies ?

speechtext: I would not permit the Minister of Agriculture to answer, because it would be out of order.

I think. Mr. Chairman, that it is only fair that you should allow the Minister of Agriculture to answer a simple question. You seem to have more control over him than his colleagues have.

I find no fault with Mr. Foley's salary. If the minister considers him a good man and worthy of the salary I don't object. I know the minister has a good staff of officers, as I said in this parliament some years ago. Here we have a vote for sundries, and I ask the minister if he could not take out of it a certain sum to meet the

[DOT]expense of these farmers who assemble in conventions, with the object of advancing the trade and prosperity of the country.

These sundries are for such things as postage, telegrams, and travelling expenses of officers. Notwithstanding the increase of the general work we have been struggling to keep within this sum which is the same as has been voted for many years. I would only he too glad to do something to bring farmers to agricultural gatherings, and we already do a great deal in this direction, but I fear we cannot undertake such a scheme as the hon. gentleman (ilr. Hackett) proposes.
Mr. SPROUT,E. This vote is to pay the expenses of high salaried officials, and it seems to me you ought to be able to do something to reduce the expenses of the farmers who travel to these conventions in the general interest of the public.
AVe do that in some other ways.
AVliy do you want three more third-class clerks ?

Under theAet of last year we got power to make temporary clerks permanent, and I wish to avail of it to do something for deserving clerks.
Archives, $12,000.
Have you appointed an archivist, and who is he ?

If I can speak confidentially to my hon. friend, I may say that I have made a recommendation, but my deputy reminds me that we have received no word from the Privy Council that the appointment has been made.
I understand that some time ago a gentleman in Quebec was appointed, and he objected on the ground that the salary was too large.
No.
Or, was not large enough; is he the same man ?
Yes.
Have you a building set apart for the purpose ?
No ; the archives office is in the Langevin block.
Do you keep adding to it all the time ?

Yes ; there is constant work going on in Paris and London, copying documents' relating to the history of Canada. AA'e also make occasional purchases of documents which are brought to our attention connected with the history and records of the country.

AArill the minister give us an idea of the number of places to which Mr. HACKETT.
the report of the archivist is sent ? Is it sent to the high schools, for instance ?
No. The number of copies issued has not been increased.
The hon. gentleman's attention was called two years ago to the propriety of sending copies to our high schools, lias he done anything in that direction ?
I confess that, if that is the case, the matter has escaped my memory.

Has the hon. minister a regular mailing list for the report ? I had a letter recently from a medical man asking me to endeavour to have his name put on the mailing list. If the minister has such a list, perhaps he will be kind enough to put this gentleman's name on If I give it to him ?

There is a list, and I shad be only too glad to add to it the name of the hon. gentleman's friend. We have never refused to put on the list the name of any one who has shown enough interest in it to ask.
Does this vote pay the salaries of any of the officers ?

I may say that this vote was increased last session, when I explained to the House that on the death of the late Dr. Brymner, who had been archivist for many years, it was thought by the government best to increase the office and give increased duties to the archivist. There has been in the Secretary of State's office a keeper of records, with two clerks under him. There are in the different departments a large number of papers and documents relating to the history of the country, to titles, and to various other things in connection with public affairs. These are scattered in a great number of different places, some not in Ottawa at all. I had thought for a long time, and the government agreed with me, that all these documents ought to be collected into one place, classified and catalogued, and put in charge of some one person who would be responsible for their safekeeping, so that they would be available to persons who wished to examine them. The death of Dr. Brymner was thought to be a suitable occasion for doing this, and It is to my regret that there has been a delay in consequence of our not being able to secure the services of such a man as I thought competent for the work. I am glad to say that 1 have now secured the services of such a man, and I hope that in a few days Air. Doughty will be able to take charge of the office and proceed with the work. That will undoubtedly involve a very considerable addition to the vote for the archives. This item was increased last session by $3,000 with that view ; but as we have not yet undertaken that work to any extent, the expenditure does not reach anywhere near $12,000, so that a large part of the vote will lapse at the end of the present fiscal year.

Under civil government we have the salary of the archivist as chief clerk ; A. Duff at $1,050 ; a binder, who binds the documents, at $804 ; Miss McCoy, stitcher, at $300 ; a Miss M. Casey, a clerk, at $600. We devote $4,000 a year to copying in London and Paris ; and during the past year we had a balance of $6,296, the great bulk of which will not be expended in the current fiscal year, but a part of which has been expended for papers and documents. Quite recently, in consequence of the lamented death of the late Senator Masson and the auction of a portion of his property, there was put up for sale at public competition a number of most interesting and valuable papers connected with the early history of this country I knew something of them, and I had them carefully investigated by experts ; and, notwithstanding pretty keen competition from Americans and others, we were able to secure all the documents that we thought of interest to Canada at a reasonable price, though nowhere near the historical value of the documents. We spent at the public auction about $500 ; but we have also made an arrangement with the family for getting a large number of other documents which were not put up at auction, for about $500 more. So that for $1,000 we have secured for the archives some most valuable papers.
I understand that the minister has in Prance some person copying important documents. When will that work be completed ?

I do not think it will ever be completed. There is an enormous mass of documents in France, in La Bibliotheque Nationale, which relate to the history of Canada. Only a small portion have been copied up to the present. We devote a certain sum every year, some $4,000, and I am not sure how much goes to Paris and how much to London.
How many officials are engaged ?
None. There are only what are called official copyists, people authorized by the authorities to make copies in the library, and who are paid by the folio.
How many ?

Sometimes one, sometimes three or four, according to circumstances. In London, I think, six are employed all t the time. There is a Mr. Tantet, who is ' officially connected with the library at Paris, who gets the work done at so much a folio. We do not know the people who do it.
He is our special official over there ?

No, he is not our official, but an official of the library. I was under the impression that he got a small honorarium for looking after this work, but I find that he charges nothing and that everything we pay is paid out by him to the copyists. The accounts are sent to the High Commissioner's office and dealt with there. [DOT] We transmit $4,000 a year to the High Commissioner to spend in London and Paris on this work.

The work is very valuable, and I would not begrudge any expense in connection with it. I am glad to know that the hon. gentleman is having copies made of documents relating to the early history of this country. Those documents are yearly growing scarcer and are liable to destruction by fire. Consequently they should be gathered up and preserved by the nation in a fireproof building. The original documents are almost priceless, and I trust that they are stored where they are absolutely safe.
These documents are stored in the Langevin block, which, though not absolutely fireproof, is more nearly so than any other public building in Ottawa.
You should take a vote for a new building.

I may do so before the end of the session. I have been waiting until the plans for the national museum and art gallery are completed. In that building there will be fireproof accommodation for the records and archives. I am seriou'sly considering also whether it would not be well, as that building cannot possibly be completed in less than two. or three years, if begun at once, to devote a sum of money for the purpose of erecting a small building absolutely fireproof, in which we might store these valuable documents, pending the completion of the national museum, and I may ask a vote for that purpose this session.
What are the qualifications of the gentleman who has been appointed Dominion Archivist ?
The gentleman appointed is Mr. A. G. Doughty, who is well known among students of our history, as having published one of the most important works on that subject, published in late years.
In collaboration with somebody ?

Yes, with Mr. Geo. Par-malee, secretary of the Education Department, but I think I may, without any disparagement to Mr. Parmalee, say that Mr. Doughty himself is the one who principally inspired that work. He is a graduate of Oxford University and consequently holds the highest credentials as an educated man. He has been in this country some seventeen or eighteen years and has been in the employ of the Quebec government as assistant librarian of the parliamentary library at Quebec. He has been engaged in historical researches in all his spare time during that period. He has

written many articles on various historical _ subjects. He has issued one or two other books on historical matters and is an enthusiast in this work. I first became acquainted with him on a visit he made here to investigate our archives. He was able to discover a number of papers in the different departments which no one in Ottawa apparently knew the existence of. He found references to them in other documents and ferreted them out. He has also a very extensive correspondence with the custodians of historical documents in the various continental cities, in London, and all over England. He has made researches in a great many well-known libraries in private houses in England, and has correspondence with the owners of these and with writers on kindred subjects. I have no hesitation in saying that Mr. Doughty stands out as probably the most qualified man for this position in the Dominion.

I have seen the work to which the hon. Minister refers. While it may be very valuable as a book of reference, it can scarcely be commended for its literary style. But we have in our province a gentleman quite as well qualified for that position, a native born Canadian, which I trust will not be a disqualification. He is a historian who has published many valuable histories, notably the war of 1812. I allude to Dr. James Hannay, a man of wide reading and knowledge, a man in every way splendidly qualified for this position. So it is not necessary for the minister to take a man outside of the native born for this office. As I say, I have nothing to say disparaging of Mr. Doughty. I read his book and thought it valuable. But I think that the claims of Dr. Hannay, as a native born Canadian, a historian of eminence, and historian of Canada, were far greater than those of Mr. Doughty, and I am very sorry the hon. minister did not appoint him. I do not speak in this way because Dr. Hannay is on my side in politics, for he is not. If he were, that would be a still greater qualification. But I speak this in simple justice to a man who has made an international reputation for himself as a historian of Canada. I think it unfortunate that he was not appointed to this important position. For, I regard it as a very important position indeed, and I think it would be more becoming that the holder of that position should not be a mere clerk in any department, but that the service of which he is the head should be a sub-department by itself.

I notice that some of the expenditures for newspapers seem large. Is more than one copy of some newspapers taken ? I find that the Toronto ' Globe ' received $8 while the ' Mail and Empire ' received $4.

Certain old established newspapers of Canada are deposited in the Mr. FISHER.
archives regularly, and have been since the first establishment of the office. The files of these are kept up without reference to newspapers or anything else.
I see that the St. John 'Telegraph ' received $16.
My officer informs me that sometimes a bill comes in for several years' subscription at once. That seems to have happened in the case referred to. Only one copy is taken.
A Mr. Richard was employed in Paris in connection with the copying of documents. What has become of him ?

He came back about seven or eight months ago, and I regret to say that, about a month or six weeks ago, he died.	.
Patent Record, ?17,000.
There is an increase here of $5,000. How is that accounted for ?

In the first place there is an increase in the number of patents, and in the second place there has been an increase in the charges of the Printing Bureau. The whole of this money is paid, to the Printing Bureau for printing the ' Record.'
What is the increase in the number of patents ?

I might first explain that this increase of $5,000 has not occurred suddenly this year ? For last year I asked for $12,000, but I shall be obliged to ask for a supplementary vote of $5,000. The estimate of $17,000 now under discussion is based upon the actual expenditure of last year. Last year there were 5,912 applications for patents, 5,673 patents were issued and 432 certificates, or a total of 6,105 documents issued which have to be recorded. In addition, there is an increase in the trade marks and designs, which are also published in the ' Patent Record,' and all the issues of copyright also. These add to the number of pages in the ' Patent Record ' and ' so increase the cost. There is also an increase in the scale of charges in the Printing Bureau.
The hon. gentleman has not told us what the increase in the issue of patents for last year was.
For the year ending 31st December last, there were 6,105 and for the year before 4,901, an increase for last year of 1.204.
Does this mean that an increased number of the ' Patent Record ' is circulated ?

No. The number printed is 1,200 copies a mouth. The distribution generally was as follows : Free libraries in

Great Britain, 61 ; foreign free-libraries, 63 : departmental list, Ottawa, 29 ; members of parliament. 213 ; senators. 77 ; free libraries in Canada, 84 ; free libraries in United States, 42 ; paid subscribers. 191-a total of 760 disposed of last year. We are constantly having demands for copies of tlie ' Patent Record ' of years back.
The bound volumes ?
They are fastened together, but not bound. We charge $2 a year.
It is a monthly production ?

Yes.
Mi1. BLAIN. How near up-to-date is it kept ?
The number for February has been issued.
Are there any bound volumes of the ' Patent Record ' in the department ?
We keep our own file bound.
But none in circulation in that form ?
No, they are simply in paper form.
Is the 'Patent Record' of assistance in the classification of the patents that the hon. gentleman has adopted in order to make the work of reference more easy.
The record is published in consecutive numbers. It is published every month and includes only the patents that were granted in the month.
But at the end of the year ?
We have not undertaken to classify them in the record ; they are classified in the office.
It seems to me that if it w'ere classified in the office it would not be a very expensive matter to classify them in the record.
There is an index to the annual volume but of course the annual volume is simply the monthly issues bound together. We do not undertake to do anything except to make an index.
In the United States they have the bound volume and the index following consecutively.
Just the index of each volume. We have that too.
It would really amount to twelve monthly records.

Twelve monthly records and at the end the index to the twelve
months. At the end of the year the index is sent forward to subscribers with the last monthly record, but of course they have to bind the volumes themselves.

In the monthly issue would not it be a very easy matter to arrange the patents under the various classes? Such an arrangement would be quite as valuable to the public as to the department, if not more so.

I think it would be possible to add to the description of each patent a statement of what class and sub-class it is placed in but to arrange the patents in classes at the end of the year would be simply to print the whole record.
You could put in the index at the en'd of the year what class each patent was placed in.

I will see if that cannot be done.
Collection and compilation of Criminal Statistics, $2,000.

The increase here is due partly to an apparent increase in crime ; that is, an increased number of cases in the returns sent in, but it is also due partly to the increased number of returns sent in. There is an increase in the organized territories and in the number of judicial officers. These returns are made by the clerks of the courts all over the country. By the statute they are required to send in their returns. They get a dollar for the return whether it contains no cases or fifty eases, and then they are allowed five cents for each indicated case, and two cents for each summary conviction. That is fixed by1 statute,
I have no control over that.
I notice you have three or four officers in different cou|nties sending in these returns.
According to the number of courts. Wherever there is a clerk of the court the returns are sent in.
Or a police magistrate.
I suppose so. The increase is due to the establishment of more courts and also apparently to tlie increased number of offences reported.
Where are these courts being increased ?
In what were the unorganized districts but are now organized. Some are in the Northwest Territories, some in the new parts of Ontario and perhaps some in the new parts of Quebec.
Do you get a summary conviction by magistrates ?
Yes, where there is an increase ill the number of courts or in magistrates' work.
I see that the amount of the vote was not all used last year, and that still you are asking for an increase this year.

That was the year before, but I am informed this year that, although we asked for the same amount as for the year before, this will not be enough, and that we wiil have to ask for a supplementary vote.
Statistical Year-book. $6,000.
This is a large increase.

Yes, I am asking for $1,000 more.
Mr. JABEiL ROBINSON. I want to congratulate the hon. Minister of Agriculture upon adding $1,000 to the vote for the Statistical Year-book, because I think this is one of the most valuable publications issued by the government, and I only hope that the hon. minister will have that book placed in the hands of all the school teachers. They think a great deal of it, and I hope they will be able to get it.

I sympathize with my hon. friend (Mr. Robinson), but I hardly think we can undertake to place it in the hands of all the teachers. That would be a pretty large contract, and we have not made provision for it.

I understand that these books cost about fifty cents each. X do not think the money could be better expended than in supplying this information to the teachers. If the teachers get it the children will get it.

There is a permanent list In the department of institutions to which it is sent. Eight hundred and forty-seven copies are sent to newspapers, 335 to libraries, not including libraries which are on the permanent list, 147 to boards of trade, 126 to electrical and steam railway companies and offices, 100 to city governments, mayors, clerks, &c.,	190 to banks, 36
to sheriffs, 117 to Supreme Court and other judges, 36 to immigration and commercial agents of the government, 75 to Dominion executive and private secretaries, 02 to provincial executives and 164 to foreign consuls in Canada. These are evidently some they have asked for to be sent off. To the High Commissioner in England, for distribution, 550 copies are sent : British ambassadors and consuls, 105 copies. To those on the permanent list, that is various institutions, mechanics' institutes and others, we send 491 copies of the Yearbook without any demand or request ; to senators, 61 copies ; telephone companies. 44 ; insurance companies, 100 ; deputy ministers, 120 ; members of parliament, 5 copies each, one bound and four in paper, 790 in all ; Minister of Agriculture's office, for dis-Mr. FISHER.
tribution, 110. I may say that this is due to requests that come in personally to me, I give an order to the office to send them. I have always sent the Year-book to anybody who asks for it. Then there is the library of parliament, 50 ; last year, Japan exhibition, 108 ; various members of the clergy, 42 ; chambers of commerce in Australia, 12 : and to various persons whose names are not on the permanent list, 1,193. No, they were not. They are not printed in that language or any other foreign language. The French edition was distributed as follows : Senators and members, 490 : legislative council, 18 ; legislative assembly, 63 ; judges, 34 ; newspapers. 70 : libraries, 37 ; council of agriculture of Quebec, 6 ; clergy, convents, colleges and chambers of commerce, &c., 110 ; barristers, notaries and other applicants, 582 ; total, 1,410.
