I would like to have the hon. Minister of Agriculture put the high school teachers in the province of Ontario, at any rate, on the list, and I think it would be well that the high school teachers throughout the Dominion should also receive a copy if it is possible.
I would be very glad to try and find out how7 many there are of such teachers, and if it is possible to supply them with this book I will be very glad to do so.

If the work is going to be authentic, I w7ould back up what my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) says, but I think I have a very vivid recollection that a year or two ago. when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was speaking on the budget and quoting from this Year-book in support of his contention, he w7as actually told by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that the figures in the Year-book were absolutely incorrect. If we are going to discuss budgets and other important matters that are necessary to be discussed in this House, and which clearly should be discussed by the people and their representatives, I think we should have a different system of getting out this Year-book, a more accurate system, so that it wall not be said again by the oldest minister of the Crown in the House, one who is certainly supposed to be an authority on trade and commerce, and wdio used to have the name of being a very great financier, that the figures in the Year-book are absolutely incorrect. I would urge the hon. Minister of Agriculture to see that the Year-book is more carefully gotten up than it appears to have been in the past, so that we will not have that sort of thing said in this House,

and so that we will have a Year-book which is accurate. It is said that this Year-book should be disseminated more freely. I am not in favour of disseminating it at all, because I do not want to send untrue and incorrect information through the country, taking the statement of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce for that. I would rather that the people had no Yearbook at all than the one which the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce says contains figures which are incorrect.
Was the statement of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce wrong or were the figures wrong ?
I know that the statement of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce was correct. The figures were incorrect in the Year-book.

I think we should have some assurance from the hon. Minister of Agriculture that that state of affairs is not going to continue ; otherwise, I would move to strike this item out altogether. We do not want to waste the money of the country by paying it out to misinform the people in regard to public affairs.
It will be my utmost endeavour to see that the figures in the Yearbook are correct.
The hon. gentleman is speaking generally, I understand. This happened to be an error that crept in.
The figure referred to by my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was incorrect.
Outside of that the book was fairly correct ?
I have not examined it in detail. There have been other occasions upon which discrepancies and inaccuracies have crept in.
Are we to understand that the book is fairly correct ?
I would not allow it to be issued unless it were fairly correct. I have had inaccuracies brought to my attention in different years, and the matter the hon. gentleman referred to was inaccurate.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce, referring to the Statistical Yearbook said :
I do not suppose that many members of this House are likely to make statements, and quote figures from a document such as the Statistical Year-hook.
And he went on to leave the impression that the figures contained in the Year-book were incorrect, and were not such as the members of this House could rely on. It is only fair that the minister should say to the House that the figures are correct with the exception of such unintentional errors 87

as do creep into all public documents. The general impression in the country is, that the Statistical Year-book is accurate, and everybody was surprised to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce cast such a reflection on this important document.

The Minister of Agriculture is not justified in saying that the figures in dispute were incorrect in the Statistical Year-book. There was a contention between the hon. member for Pictou and the Min- * ister of Trade and Commerce, and both claimed the victory. It is not fair for the Minister of Agriculture to say, that one of his chief officers was all wrong in the case, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was all right. I am not prepared to say whether the figures were correct or incorrect, and unless the Minister of Agriculture has studied the matter carefully, he is , not warranted in saying that the figures were incorrect.
The hon. gentleman says there was a controversy in which each thought he came off the better ; I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce came off the better.
And on that, you based the statement that the statistican was wrong.
I think so.

Then we are to understand that the Minister of Agriculture, after listening to the discussion, and without any bias, of course( in favour of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, came to the conclusion without studying the matter for himself, that one of his chief officers was all wrong. The explanation will let the country know that the Minister of Agriculture knows nothing at all about it.

When we take up a blue-book we expect to find it accurate. It is a humiliating admission for a minister to make, that any document got up under his authority is unreliable. If the information is not accurate, the money is simply wasted.
The minister should verify those documents before he allows them to be issued.
I shall try to do-so.
Are the statistics given in the Year-book brought down to the 30th of June ?

The information given in the Year-book is taken from the annual reports of the different departments, and it is brought down to various dates. For instance the customs figures are to the 30th of June, and the agricultural figures are to the 1st of November.
The information we get in it is almost a year old.
Yes.
We have monthly returns from the Customs Department and conse-
quently the information in the Year-book is almost useless.
What is this increase of $1,000 for ?
I was asked in the House last year to increase the edition, and the increased appropriation is for that purpose.
Could not the figures in the Statistical Year-book be given, up to a uniform date V

In the Department of Agriculture, for instance, the exports of cattle are given up to the close of navigation, and these figures are incorporated in the Yearbook. When the Statistical Year-book is made up, it takes these figures in that form ; but it deals with the figures connected with the trade and navigation or trade and commerce reports to the end of the fiscal year.
Does the Year-book contain a copy of the customs tariff of Canada ?

No, the Statistical Yearbook is not intended to contain copies of such things. It is a compilation of tables made up from the different reports, and I do not think it would be advisable as a general rule to publish the same thing over and over.
There is a good deal of repetition in it, such as the returns of different years.
That is for purposes of comparison.

I think it might very properly contain the Canadian customs tariff and also the United States customs tariff. These are documents to which the average business man refers very frequently, and I think it would be a great convenience to have them both published in this book.
I will discuss that with the statistician.

Would it not be possible to have the statistical Year-book correspond with the fiscal year ? The tables published in it are likely to be quite misleading when compared with other reports if they do not correspond with the reports ending the 30th Jyme.

The hon. gentleman's suggestion is a good one, and I will see if it can be arranged. No doubt confusion has sometimes arisen from quotations from the Year-book and quotations from the blue book failing to agree.

I understood the minister to say that in the report of the Department of Agriculture the exports of cattle were given up to the 1st of November in each year. If so, a person reading it and the table in the Year-book would be badly mixed, because the table in the Year-book gives the exports to the end of the 30th of June.

I would like to ask whether the government have under their control any system of obtaining the vital statistics of the country-the births, marriages and deaths. While the subject of vital and all other statistics is assigned by the British North America Act to the Dominion of Canada, some of the provinces do attempt to obtain these statistics ; but having no authority by law to do so, they cannot impose any legal penalties upon the people who refuse to give statistics of that kind. I know what I am speaking about, because very lately in my own province an attempt was made to coerce physicians into reporting the births which occurred in their practice. I think the only way these statistics can be obtained in a reliable form is by the Department of Agriculture instituting some system of collecting them. I would like to have the opinion of the minister on that subject, and an expression of the intention of the government with regard to it. I think it is extremely important that we should have vital statistics as well as other statistics. It is a matter which belongs exclusively to the parliament of Canada and does not belong to the various provinces of Canada. Although some of the provinces are obtaining statistics, they cannot be accepted as reliable, because the province have not the power to enforce any law they may have on the subject.
They do enforce a Registration Act, under which they demand the registration of births, deaths and marriages, and impose a penalty for neglect to register.

There was a penalty imposed under a similar Act in my own province, but when the parties who had the administering of the law attempted to collect the penalty, they found that they were immediately out of court, and could not do it.

I am rather surprised at the information which the hon. gentleman has given the committee. I thought this question of vital statistics was referred to the provincial authorities. I know that some of the provinces collect them. We find on page 642 the births, deaths and marriages in Canada, and we find that these are not given in some of the provinces because no register of these is kept there. That does not necessarily prove that there is not legal power in the provincial legislatures to pass laws on these subjects. There is no doubt that the collection of statistics is within the purview of the parliament of Canada and the power for that purpose is granted the Department of Agriculture. It would be quite within my rights as minister to make arrangements for the collection of statistics of that kind. I believe that a very considerable enlargement of the statistical work of my department would be in the public in-

terest. It is a matter to which I have given some consideration. We have censuses every ten years in which we get all the information on these matters, but between the census we have apparently little direct information of this hind.

In Ontario we havq_re-gistration offices in which marriages, deaths and births must be registered. That is as far as the province can go, but as regards the collection of statistics, that belongs to the federal parliament.

In the province of Quebec we have a similar registration law and besides vital statistics are collected by the Bureau of Health under the charge of Dr. Da Chappelle. This bureau collects very valuable statistics.
We have the same in Ontario.
No. Sometimes a request is sent in to the statistician for information on some particular subject. He frequently prepares such information and these men would help to prepare it.
The expenditure last year on the Year-book was $4,555 and on general statistics, $2,453 or a total of $6,895. The estimate this year is $9,200, or an increase of thirty per cent.

This is entirely paid to the Printing Bureau for turning out the book. If we get more copies, we have to pay more, and I am asking for an increase this year for the purpose of getting more. As to this item for general statistics, it is an item that has been there ever since I took office. Sometimes it is not all spent and sometimes it is. It goes to pay the salaries of men who are practically permanent who have been in the service ever since I became minister.
This is a considerable increase over the expenditure of last year.
Mr. Watts, who was employed on the census during the compilation of the census, now returns to this staff.
Did not the minister need him on the statistical staff while the census was being compiled? I suppose he will be useful when another census comes on.
He was on the staff when the previous census was prepared.
He has been in the department with Mr. Johnson for many years.

Yes, since 1881.
Aid to agricultural societies, $7,000.
How is this managed 7

This is spent entirely in the Northwest Territories. In that part of the country, the Dominion takes the place, to a considerable extent, of the provincial government. This sum has appeared in the estimates for twelve or fifteen years. The money is divided among the agricultural societies in the Northwest Territories pro rata according to their membership. Each society sends in a list of its members, and this $7,000 is divided pro rata.
How many societies were there last year 7
Sixteen.
There were twenty the year before.
Would the hon. minister please name the societies 7

Fairmede, Lome, Lethbridge, Lacombe, Maple Creek, Moose Moun-

tain, Medicine Hat, Moosomin, Regina, Rosthern and Hague, Sterling, South Edmonton, Centre Assiniboia, Inter-Western Pacific, Yorkton, and Edmonton Industrial Exposition Association.
How is it that $203 was paid out to the Macleod District Association the year before last, and none last year ? Is there no society there ?
They have disbanded or have been joined to some other society. Every society that sends in its returns gets its share, but if a society does not comply with this rule it gets nothing.
Why is the amount stationary year after year ? Can the minister tell us what was the membership of these societies ten years ago, say, and last year ?

The amount is fixed at $7,000, and it is distributed among the societies. If there is a large aggregate membership so much, less is paid per member. I have not the details here to make a comparison of the membership in previous years and last year. I may say that until two or three years ago these societies made their returns to the department direct, but, since then the returns have been made to the Territorial Department of Agriculture, and have been forwarded by them to us, they, dealing with the organization of these societies under an ordinance of the territorial government.
The number of societies seems to be fewer last year than the year before. Can the minister explain that ?
The territorial government have been discouraging the formation of district agricultural societies, trying to get them to amalgamate, so that there might not be so many rival organizations.
It would be interesting to know the membership of these sixteen societies of last .year and the twenty societies of the year before.
I have not the figures at hand.
I suppose the figures are in the department. Would the hon. minister kindly make a note of it and be prepared to give details on a future occasion ?
Is any aid given to the different agricultural societies in the provinces ?

No.
Experimental farms, $100,000.

I will not ask the committee to take up this vote to-night. The report of the Experimental Farm has not been laid upon the table. It has been in the hands of the printers for months, and I am told that it will be ready in a few days. I will not ask>
that the vote be Mr. FISHER.
gone on with until the report is before the House. But perhaps the committee would consider the next item :
Printing and distribution of reports and bulletins of farms, $7,000.
This is a subsidiary item to the farm vote. If hon. gentlemen agree, this item can be passed, but with the understanding that any question arising out of it can be discussed, if necessary, on the farm vote.
This is a very important item, and one on which there will be a considerable discussion, by reason of certain things that have occurred this year.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) objects to passing the item, I will not pass it. But, I thought we might pass the item and so dispose of it, with the full understanding that, on the farm vote, if any hon. gentleman wishes to bring up any question in relation to the bulletins, it could be discussed then.
I only draw the minister's attention to the fact that some gentlemeu desire to speak on this item who are not here this evening.

Well, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) prefers, we will not pass the item.
Toward compiling historical data with regard to the Acadian families in Canada, $1,400.
Would the hon. minister explain why this work is not done in connection with the archives ?

It is an entirely different thing. It has been a special vote for a number of years back, similar to a vote taken a few years ago for a similar compilation in reference to the names of French Canadians in Quebec. This is somewhat kindred in nature to the archives vote, but the work is done in a special way by a special officer appointed for that purpose and is not intended to be a permanent work. If it had been intended to be a permanent vote it should be under the archives, but it is a temporary expenditure that will probably only go on for a couple of years.
It seems to me permanent enough and to have gone on for some years.
Three or four years.
What is the object of this work ?

It is the result of a request on the part of the Acadians that the records of their families should be preserved for reference. I think the request was based on a similar work performed many years ago on behalf of the French Canadian families in Quebec. This matter came up some four year ago and the members of the House on both sides who represented Acadia presented a request to me and through

me to ttie government to undertake this work. It was thought advisable to do so. and Mr. Gaudet was recommended by them to do the work. He has been engaged on it for some time, and I am informed that he has the first volume practically ready for the printer.	~
Is there any return of any data already collected ?
His work is in the compilation of the volumes and there have been no interim reports of any kind.
I understood the minister to say that Mr. Gaudet would prosecute the work.
Yes.
How far has he proceeded ?

I am informed that he has the first volume just about ready for the printer. There will probably be three volumes but the work which has been done is largely for all three volumes so that the second two volumes will not take relatively as long in preparation as the first volume.
Mr, HACKETT. I know Mr. Gaudet very well and have known him for nearly a quarter of a century and I can say that there could be no more competent man to do the work, than Mr. Gaudet.
He was recommended to me as such.

The expulsion of the Acadians from Nova Scotia in the 18th century is a most interesting chapter in Canadian history. Those people have been scattered all over the continent of America from Louisiana to Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island, and although expelled from their homes they have proven that they have the ability to succeed in all portions of the North American continent where they have settled. It is interesting to read that these people who were shipped from Nova Scotia to Louisiana, carrying with them their mother tongue of old France, have retained that tongue. I see here in the ' Citizen ' of today an article headed :

Washington * Post.'
Congressman Broussard, of Louisiana, never spoke any English until he came to Georgetown university at the age of 15, and even now he probably uses his mother tongue-French- with the greater fluency.
'It is a curious thing,' said Mr. Broussard,
' how the French language has remained the dominant tongue in my home country. Brought there by Acadians of Nova Scoita in the eighteenth century, it prevails to-day, and I be-live always will. Curiously enough, you will find plenty of men in my district with such unmistakable- English names as Jones and Hayes who can't read, speak or write a word of English. Still funnier is the talk of the black people. Their negro-French would be unintelligible in Paris, yet it is the softest, sweetest, most musical speech I ever heard from human lips. It knows no grammar, but it is the very essence of euphony and melody.'
These people were driven from Nova Scotia in the 18th century. and have settled all along the North American continent. I think it is a great work for our Canadian government to ascertain as nearly as possible the number of Acadian families who were expelled in the first place from Grande Pr§e in Nova Scotia and then- descendants to-day in this country. I am sure there is not a member in this House who will say one word in opposition to the vote that is being asked for this record.
Fumigating stations, $4,000.
'Mr. DANIEL. Where are these stations ?

There is one in Vancouver, B.C., one in Winnipeg, Man., two in Ontario, at Windsor and Niagara Falls, one in Quebec, at St. Johns and one in New Brunswick, at St. John. The one at St. John, N.B., serves practically for the maritime provinces. These stations are necessary to protect nursery stock in this country against the increase of the San Jose scale, an insect pest which affects the trees in the United States very considerably and which we are trying to keep out of this country. An Act was passed five or six years ago and at first absolute prohibition of the importation of these trees was enforced. That was modified a year afterwards by the establishment of these few stations where nursery stock can be brought in and fumigated and then allowed to be distributed. That modification was made in the interest of the trade and of the people of Canada who wished to buy United States stock. The fumigation is considered to be an absolute insecticide for the scale and the result is that trees, after being fumigated, are absolutely safe even when they may have been affected by the scale.
Has the hon. gentleman any information as to how manv trees were imported through these stations'?
I could not tell that. By reference to the customs returns I could see how many packages, but I could not give the number of trees.

I would like to know a little about the system that is in vogue in regard to the fumigating of trees. Perhaps the hon. minister would tell us at what seasons of the year this fumigating is done.
I notice, at Page D-28 of the Auditor General's report, that Mr. O. N. Garner was employed for two months to December 7, 1902 and two months to May 15, 1903. Does that mean that there was no inspection or fumigation excepting between October 7th and December 7th and March 15th and May

15th ? What would be done with the trees shipped in at any other time of the year ?

They could not be fumigated. Any fumigating that is done must take place when the plant is dormant. If the fumigating were done after the plant starts to grow it would kill it. These are the dates between which it will be safe to fumigate the plant.
That is to save the plant ?
Yes.
Wrhat is the object of the fumigating ? Suppose a man brings in trees at any other time of the year that require fumigating ?
He can only bring them in during these seasons.
By what regulation is that governed ?
By Order in Council under the Act which authorizes the Governor in Council to fix the dates for fumigating these plants.
Does the hon. minister say that at Niagara Falls plants are not brought in except during these four months ?
Yes.
I am afraid that the hon. minister will find that there are plants brought in at other seasons of the year.

The hon. gentleman need not fear because the customs officials will look after that. Instructions have been sent out to every customs house officer not to allow plants of this character to be brought in except at these dates.
I live in the Niagara district, and I think the hon. minister had better see that his instructions are more effectively carried out. My information is not the same as that of the hon. gentleman.
I would bq, very glad if the hon. gentleman would give any information which would lead to the detection of any violation of the law.
These plants are being brought in at times other than during these four months.
I have never heard that before.
I have.
Against what countries is this regulation enforced ?

Against the United States and Japan. I am not certain about any other countries than these two. I think the Hawaiian islands and possibly some other southern countries are also included. But Mr. LANCASTER.
the countries from which we fear contagion are the United States and Japan.
What is the condition at the present time 1 Is the disease increasing or diminishing ?

I think it is decreasing. Before the Act was passed prohibiting importation except in this way there was some scale, though not much, in the country. The provincial authorities have undertaken to stamp it out. I think Ontario is the only province where it is recognized or known to exist. The provincial authorities of Ontario have attempted to stamp it out. They have adopted several regulations. We have not undertaken to interfere with any internal trade between the provinces. We have no means of preventing it, but we have means, through the customs, of preventing the importation of plants affected with scale, we have been trying to do so and I think we have succeeded. There has not been any case of scale in Canada that it has even been suggested came across the frontier since the passage of this Act.
Would the hon. minister state whether the trade in respect to the importation of trees between the United States and Canada is increasing ?

I could not give that in detail because I have not the figures showing the importation of trees. I think there has been a larger number imported as time has gone on, because our people have been planting orchards very much more freely during the last year or two than they were five or six years ago when this Act was introduced. While, of course, the introduction of such trees has been very seriously impeded by the operations of this Act, I think, that, as years go by, the facilities are being better understood, that people are perhaps importing a few more and that there is a greater demand for nursery stock in Canada than ever before. But this has been to a great extent met by the greater production of nursery stock. There is a larger number of nurseries in Canada producing good stock than ever before.

I do not know quite what the hon. gentleman means by saying that no scale has come across the border into the Niagara district, for instance, because the information and belief we have there is that all that has come in there has come across from the United States.
I say since the operation of this Act.
You can hardly make any one believe in the Niagara district that they produce the scale there. It has always been supposed in the Niagara district that this scale came in from the United States.

That is the scale which existed before the Act came into operation,

but there has been no suggestion by anybody that I have ever heard that since the Act has been in operation any scale has been introduced into the country.

Has any person suggested to the hon. gentleman where the scale did come from since the operation of the Act ?
Mr. E1SHER. It was there before the Act was passed.
It came in before the operation of the Act and remained there ?
Yes.
Is the department taking any other steps than simply fumigating the plants ?

Nothing excepting that our entomologist at the Experimental Farm is constantly watching and giving instructions and information to farmers just as he does on other subjects connected with entomology. He attends meetings of horticulturists and fruit growers to give information in regard to scale and other pests and diseases.
I know that as far as the province of Ontario is concerned the government there have taken steps for the purpose of destroying infected trees.
Yes.
And this government in no way interferes in that matter ?
No.
Will six fumigating stations be ample for all the requirements ?
I have several requests for additional stations but none in Ontario. I have had a request for one at Victoria, Vancouver Island, and for one at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia.
Would the hon. minister give us some idea of the amount of money that is paid to foreign countries for trees that come in here ?
That information will be found in the trade and navigation returns.

I do not desii'e to find fault with the amount of salary paid to the gentleman at Niagara Falls, because, even if he did not have much to do. his time would be occupied in looking for this work during these months for which that gentleman was paid. But, I would like to know to what extent fumigating was done at Niagara Falls. This gentleman. Mr. Garner, was no doubt in readiness to do the work if it was there to be done, and I am not saying that he should not be paid his salary but I would like to know the number of trees that it was found necessary to fumigate last year.
Mr. Fletcher's report will give that information, and I will place it before the hon. gentleman later on.
Is it not a fact that the San Jose scale is decreasing ?
I believe that the efforts to stamp it out have been successful.
I think it is also a fact that there is not so much nursery stock imported now.
What is the system of fumigation with regard to nursery stock grown in Canada ?

The Ontario authorities see that no nursery stock is sent out of that province until it has been fumigated.
To assist in the holding of a Dominion exhibition in the city of Winnipeg during the year 1904, $50,000.

This is in continuance of the policy adopted last year when we gave a vote to the Toronto Industrial exhibition to make it of a Dominion character. A request was made that Winnipeg should be treated in the same way this year, and the representations made on behalf of that exhibition were such as to justify us, as we thought, in giving the same grant as was given to Toronto. The Winnipeg exhibition is the exhibition of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories ; it is a very large enterprise, excellently well managed for many years and is representative of that part of our Dominion between Lake Superior and the Rocky Mountains. We thought that an extra effort might be made at this year's exhibition not only to show the newcomers into the Northwest and Manitoba the resources of the country and our system of agriculture, but also to impress on the large number of visitors who come from the United States, the fertility of the country, in the hope that the stream of immigration from the south may be continued.
When will the Winnipeg exhibition take place ?
The latter part of July.
Is it the intention to adjourn the House so that the members may go ?
I hope the hon. gentlemen opposite will let us away before that.
From whom did the request for this grant come ?

The request came from the authorities of the Winnipeg exhibition primarily, and I understand that it was supported by the whole public opinion of that section of Canada by communications, directed generally to the Minister of the Interior. The matter came direct to Council, and it was dealt with by Council. I can say with full confidence that the Winnipeg exhibition is endorsed and supported by the whole public opinion of that western country.
Perhaps the Minister of the Interior has some explanation to give.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There were two special features in connection with the Dominion exhibition at Winnipeg this year, which caused me to take the responsibilty of impressing upon my colleagues the desirability of making this grant. In years past applications have been made for assistance to this exhibition, but it was deemed well not to establish a precedent for similar grants in other parts of Canada. Last year, however, a precedent was created by the giving of a grant to the Toronto exhibition which was called a Dominion exhibition, in the sense that its scope was considerably enlarged by the fact that it received financial assistance from this government. It was represented that the Winnipeg exhibition this year should be specially made a means of bringing the eastern portion of and the western portion of Canada in closer touch.
Apart from matters which are in controversy between the two sides of the House, hon. gentlemen will all understand that the manufacturers of eastern Canada have been looking to the west for , an increased market for their products, so when this application was made by the secretary-treasurer of the Winnipeg Exhibition Roar'd, Mr. Heubaeh, I discussed that phase of the question with him. I said to him that I would approve of making a grant on two grounds ; one was that an exhibition of eastern manufactures should be made a special feature ; the other was that we might make the introduction of visitors from leading agricultural settlements of the United States a special feature. Mr. Heubaeh expressed the opinion that his board of directors would be quite willing to meet the conditions imposed by the government. Negotiations were opened with the secretary of the Manufacturers' Association, discussions took place between representatives of the Exhibition Board, representatives- of the Manufacturers' Association, the Minister of Agriculture and myself, with the result that the Manufacturers' Association took up very warmly the project of making a special exhibit of eastern manufactures. A special building is provided for that purpose; special regulations, the details of which I need not refer to now, have been arranged. A special feature of the exhibition will be the exhibit of Canadian manufactures under the direction of the manufacturers themselves ; and the hope and desire of the government is that in this way a stimulus may be given to the use of Canadian manufactures in the western portion of Canada by the people's observation of the excellence of the goods. The other point to which I desire to advert for a moment is what may be called the immigration feature of the exhibition. We have been carrying on a rather successful immigration work in the Western States at a considerable expenditure of money ; and Mr. FISHER.
the results achieved have been due entirely to close organization and hard work on the part of our agents. While perhaps to the outsider the movement bears some appearance of being spontaneous, that is well known to those engaged in the work to be entirely contrary to the fact. The success of the immigration movement from the Western States to the Canadian Northwest is directly due to the hard word of our agents ; and during the last year or two especially, the railway companies of the Western States, particularly those interested in the settlement of Montana, Washington Territory, some parts of Oregon and some parts of the Southwestern States, have made strong efforts to check the movement by the expenditure of very large sums of money and by the distribution of literature much of which is directly calculated to injure the reputation of our Northwest as an agricultural country. It seemed to me, therefore, that it would be a most opportune and useful thing, having in view the desirability of keeping up the movement of settlers from the Western States to our Northwest, if we could get as many representative men as possible from those localities in the Western States from which we draw our settlers, to the exhibition at Winnipeg this year, so that they could have an ocular demonstration of the capabilities of our western country. Some arrangements have already been made in the direction of securing the visit of editorial associations to the exhibition, and these arrangements will be extended between now and the time the exhibition will be held. The two features to which I have referred were those which to my mind made it especially desirable in the interest of Canada that the exhibition at Winnipeg this year should be aided by the government. The exhibition board took up the matter with great energy and enthusiasm, and I have no doubt at all that the exhibition will be made a great success. I cordially add my word to what my hon. colleague the Minister of Agriculture has said respecting the skill and ability with which this exhibition has been carried on. I very well remember when it began, and when the board came to the legislature of Manitoba for a small grant to enable it to get on its feet. It has been liberally supported b/ the local authorities-the legislature of Manitoba, the city of Winnipeg and the citizens generally; and it has been one of the important agencies in promoting the development and progress of the west in the last few years.
What is the usual grant made by the provincial government

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say what is given now. When I was a member of the provincial government, it gave $8,000 a year.
How much is Winnipeg giving this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I believe $50,000.
I understand that this exhibition is to open about the 20th of July. Is that not too early for a proper exhibit of the products of the province ?

That has been the date of the exhibition for many years. The authorities in Manitoba who have the responsibility of the exhibition have fixed on about that date, which comes between seed time and harvest, and is the most convenient time for the great mass of the population to reach it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I remember very distinctly when the question arose as to whether the fair should be held in the fall or in the summer, and it was a moot question for two or three years. Attempts were made to hold the exhibition in the fall, and they were not successful. The conditions are somewhat different there from what they are in the eastern provinces. In the fall, our farmers in the west are extremely busy. One can understand that from the time the grain becomes ripe until the snow falls, everybody on the farm is working late and early, and it has been found that the only possible hope of having a successful exhibition is to be found in holding it in the summer.

If the conditions imposed are such as to ensure that this exhibition shall have the status of a Dominion exhibition, the grant is one we should support. It seems to me, from an interview I had with the secretary of the exhibition, that the date is a little later than that mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture. The date mentioned to me was from the 25th of July until the 5th of August.
It will commence between the 20th and 30th of July.

The objects seem to be such as should commend themselves to the members of the House and the country generally, and I would not be inclined to put last among those objects the importance of having the people of the east visit, as far as may be possible, the city of Winnipeg and the west, and in that way become familiar, as they cannot otherwise, with the growing importance, not only of Winnipeg but of the Northwest country generally. It is of the utmost importance that the people of the east and the west should be brought into the closest touch and especially that the people of the eastern provinces should now and then visit Manitoba and the Northwest and understand the possibilities of that very great country. I believe that the secretary and directors and all those in charge of the exhibition are very anxious that people from the east should go there in great numbers. They have some project in view by which a number of members of
parliament should take this occasion to visit Winnipeg and the west, and as far as I am concerned I must say that I think it would be very much in the public interest if that proposal were carried out to the fullest possible extent.

It was reported in Winnipeg a few days ago that an arrangement was in contemplation by which a train should leave Halifax and take up on the way all members of parliament who could be induced to visit this exhibition. That would certainly be in harmony with the suggestion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. It is extremely desirable that every member of this House should proceed to the Northwest, even if not able to spare more time than to visit Winnipeg and portions of Manitoba. Has any such suggestion been made and under what auspices would such an excursion take place ? It certainly would be very desirable that as many as possible should visist the exposition. That would be beneficial in more ways than one. Apart from getting acquainted with the western country, knowing more of its resources, being able to legislate better in its interests, it would be an object lesson on a question much discussed in the House at present, because it would show the country the advantages to be gained if the Intercolonial should be extended into the province of Manitoba and the west. I would be very glad indeed if some arrangement could be made to have as large a deputation as possible go. west on that occasion.

I notice that we are increasing the vote some $50,000. Last year we voted $150,000, and we are now asked to vote $200,000. I am referring to the item, ' exhibitions generally ' which comes next. Care should be taken that in giving these grants, we are not encouraging one exhibition at the expense of another. If the Win, nipeg exhibition should take place in the autumn, it would interfere with the success of the Toronto exhibition.
Mr. FISHER, The item to which the hon. gentleman refers has to do with exhibitions in foreign countries.

The hon. gentleman says that the Winnipeg exhibition will begin between the 20th and 30th of July. If that be the date, the root crops will not have had time to ripen. I do not know whether it is intended to have a display of root crops or not, but I take it for granted that all agricultural products will be on exhibition.
The exhibitions in other parts of Canada are held much later in the year, so that the exhibition at Winnipeg cannot interfere with any of them.

When I spoke a moment or two ago, the minister was engaged in conversation with the Minister of

Finance and did not hear what I said. I spoke with reference to an excursion from Halifax through to Winnipeg, which, it was reported in Winnipeg a few days ago, is to take place. Would that be under the patronage of the Minister of Agriculture or be managed by those in charge of the exhibition at Winnipeg ? To my mind an excursion of that nature would result in many more members going west than if there was no organization of the kind. Has the hon. minister had any communication with the Winnipeg people on that point ?

There is no definite arrangement as far as I know. Some of the officials connected with the Winnipeg exhibition discussed that matter with the Minister of the Interior but no definite arrangement has been come to. It is a matter which the government have not undertaken to manage and control and no part of this money will be devoted to such an excursion.

I would not for a moment presume that the money we are now voting was intended to pay the expenses of an excursion to the west. I think that no member of parliament who can find time to go, now that such ample provision has been made by the Railway Act for transportation, would hesitate to pay his own expenses. No one would expect the government or the people connected with the Winnipeg exposition to pay any part of that expense.
I do not mean to suggest that any part of this money would be used to pay the expenses of members.

My impression was that if the excursion received the patronage of the Minister of Agriculture and the people of Winnipeg and the west, a great many more people would be likely to go than if no action was taken along that line.

I want to say a word with regard to Prinde Edward Island. While this exhibition may be of advantage to the people of Canada generally, it cannot bo of very much benefit to the people of Prince Edward Island. I have been advocating all evening, so far as my abilities would go, that delegates of farmers conventions should have free transportation on the railways, but I have received very little support. When you consider the excellent products that Prince Edward Island has and the fact that it is impossible for the people of that province to participate in the benefits of this exhibition in Winnipeg, it seems to me that the proposal I have to make is reasonable. I beg to move in amendment that this vote of $200,000 be reduced to $195,000 and that the sum of $5,000 be devoted by the government to the support of the provincial exhibition in Prince Edward Island for the present year.
The vote we are now discussing is for $50,000. That amendment would apply to the next item which is $200,000.
I supposed that the other item was passed, but I will leave my amendment until this item of $200,000 is before us.

I wish to ask if any rates have been arranged by the railways for conveying exhibits from the eastern provinces to this Winnipeg exhibition ? I know that in the town in which I live, there are a number of manufacturers who intend to exhibit in Winnipeg.
Mr, FISHER. Such arrangements as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) refers to are being made by the Winnipeg Exhibition officials.

I am glad to hear that, because I believe that in the eastern provinces, judging from what I hear from my own province of Nova Scotia, a large number of our manufacturers will exhibit at this Doninion exhibition. I hope my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) will not move this amendment. I think I would have about as much right to ask that the Dominion government should assist an exhibition in the county of Cumberland or in two or three counties of Nova Scotia. This exhibition in Winnipeg is a Dominion exhibition, and part of its object will be to show to the manufacturers of eastern Canada the immense heritage we have in the west. I am fully in sympathy with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) on the subject of a parliamentary excursion. I presume that, before the last of July we shall have had six or seven weeks at home, and we may be anxious to get on the wing once more, I believe that the education of a member of parliament is incomplete if he has not seen the western prairies ? It is difficult for a man to understand what the word ' Canada ' means, until he looks upon the prairies and feels himself lost in that immense heritage of ours. I have had the pleasure of being on the prairies, but have never gone to the Pacific coast. I hope to do so at an early day. I believe every member of parliament will come back a better Canadian if he can go to Winnipeg during the Dominion exhibition and learn the greatness of that city which will be the Chicago of Canada in a few years. Every encouragement should be given to members of parliament and others who assist in moulding opinion in this country, to visit the west and be impressed by the immensity of our country and the variety of its resources. This is a vote that we should heartily support.
We do.

I trust then, my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) will not bring in this amendment, making it appear that we think in provinces instead of thinking as a Dominion. The hon. member for Halton says it will be a good thing for members of parliament to go to Winnipeg during the exhibition, because they will then see the necessity for extending the Intercolonial westward. I think that the effect of such a visit upon their minds must be to convince them of the need of another transcontinental railway.

I think it is hardly fair to my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) to speak as though he were moving an amendment to this vote. The vote to which his amendment refers is the next vote of $200,000 for exhibitions.
I take it that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) is as much in favour of this Winnipeg exhibition as any other member of this House. I think all the members on this side, so far as I can gather, are in favour of it, and we should not mix up with this item an amendment which is proposed to another vote.
I think that we should pass over the next item of 'Exhibitions.' and after adopting the next item, No 48, we might adjourn.
Do I understand that the item for $200,000 is passed ?
No. We pass over that.
Why ?

Because the committee does not wish to discuss it but to take up *v otes that are not controversial.
For renewing and improving Canadian exhibit at Imperial Institute, London, $8,000.
It is now half past eleven, If the committee pass this next item, could it not be with the understanding that the question may be discussed on some other item, and then the committee to adjourn ?

There is no additional vote here, and I can give a clear explanation in a few minutes. I thought we might pass it, and then I would be glad to move as the hon. gentleman says, that the committee rise.
Could we not pass the item, but with the understanding that we may discuss the question later on ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When a resolution is passed by the committee and reported back to the House, it is taken out of the hands of the committee. If, then, we undertake to discuss an item that is passed, we discuss what has been withdrawn from us. Of course, the minister can give liberty on some other item to discuss the question. We may be a little out of
order but that is the only w7ay that it can be done. For instance, when a report is made to-night, that certain items have passed, then those items that are marked ' passed ' go into the hands of the House and cannot be dealt with further by the committee.
Perhaps it would be better to stop here because otherwise we might take up as much time in settling whether we would discuss it as would be necessary to dispose of the item finally.

I might explain that this is practically a re-vote. I gave a very full explanation last year in regard to the arrangements for the Imperial Institute and this year in consequence of the delay in the reorganization of the Imperial Institute, under the Board of Trade of the Imperial government, nothing has been done and no money has been spent up to the present time except a few dollars. This vote is to carry out the arrangement made last year under the new organization of the Imperial Institute which has now become a branch of the Imperial Board of Trade. Formerly it was under a special commission and the vote is really a re-vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.
Only upon the understanding that we can discuss it under some other item.
Any questions about it I would be glad to answer at any other time only when the item is passed it cannot be taken up again ; but I shall be very glad to give any information.
If there is any qualification, I think it should stand.
I thought there was no real need of discussing it.

I may say that one of the hon. gentlemen who is not here now asked to have it stand.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
Is it intended to take up any/ government business on Monday ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we reach government business w^e will continue supply at the point where we leave it to-night.
The estimates of the Minister of Agriculture ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, to be followed by those of the Minister of Marine and those of the Minister of Inland Revenue.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
Monday, May 9, 1904.
